questions.question: The statement that 'uncertainty itself acts as a kind of tariff' means that
options: the government in fact imposes a formal duty on any exporter who signs contracts before the agreement is concluded
exporters in rival countries are made to pay higher duties whenever the position of India's own exporters is unclear
uncertainty raises the cost of making commitments that are hard to reverse, much as a duty on trade would
uncertainty lowers the duties that exporters have to pay on goods which are shipped under contracts that were signed earlier
questions.explanation: Answer: uncertainty raises the cost of making hard-to-reverse commitments, as a duty on trade would. Why: the sentence itself explains it: exporters 'need certainty', and uncertainty raises 'the cost of commitments that cannot easily be reversed'. 'A kind of' signals a comparison, not a literal tax. Why the others fail: no formal duty is imposed, rivals' duties are not said to depend on India's position, and uncertainty is never said to lower any duties.

questions.question: The author's view on India's decision to wait is best described as
options: defensible but not free of cost, since the price of waiting has to be weighed against the risk of an illusory margin
mistaken, since the cost of waiting is certain to be greater than any margin that India could hope to gain over its rivals
wholly justified, since waiting costs exporters nothing as long as they have planned their shipments well in advance
irrelevant, since the value of a trade agreement does not in any way depend on the structure of tariffs around it
questions.explanation: Answer: defensible but not costless. Why: paragraph 3 calls waiting something a negotiator 'may rationally prefer'; paragraph 5 opens 'None of this makes the delay costless' and ends by saying the cost of waiting 'must be set against the cost of a margin that proves illusory'. Why the others fail: 'mistaken' and 'wholly justified' each ignore half of that balance; 'irrelevant' contradicts the whole argument about the tariff structure.

questions.question: Which of the following best states the main point of the passage?
options: India's record on tuberculosis is better than the figures suggest, since a fall of 38 per cent is faster than any other country has achieved
The share of the world's cases is a misleading figure that should be dropped in favour of the rate per hundred thousand people
A fall in deaths proves that tuberculosis will soon be eliminated in India, so that the burden need no longer be a cause for concern
Progress and burden are different measures that answer different questions, and sound reporting and policy require both of them
questions.explanation: Answer: progress and burden measure different things, and both are needed. Why: paragraph 2 separates change from level; paragraph 3 shows level itself has two measures; paragraph 4 says 'Which figure matters depends on who is asking'; the last paragraph says honest reporting 'would give both'. Why the others fail: the passage says the decline is faster than the world's, not than every country's; it says neither share nor rate is wrong, so dropping one is not argued; and it warns that the 'next ten per cent will not be as easy', so 'soon eliminated' is unsupported.

questions.question: The author says that 'a high starting point makes rapid improvement easier'. This is because
options: countries with a large share of the problem receive more money from international bodies than other countries do
the first gains come from reaching people who were untreated, which is cheaper than finding the hardest cases later
a high starting point means that the figures were recorded wrongly, so that any later figure is bound to look better
the world as a whole improves at the same speed as any single country, whatever its starting point happens to be
questions.explanation: Answer: early gains come from reaching the untreated, which is cheaper than finding hard cases later. Why: paragraph 2 says 'the first reductions, achieved by extending treatment to people who were previously unreached, are cheaper than the last, which require finding the hardest cases'. Why the others fail: international funding, mistaken records and equal speeds of improvement are all unmentioned. In fact the passage says India improved FASTER than the world.

questions.question: According to the passage, a country's share of the world's cases tends to be large if the country is populous because
options: populous countries are known to have weaker health systems than countries whose populations are small
the figure is always calculated by the country itself, which has a reason to overstate the extent of the disease
it is an absolute count, so that size inflates it regardless of the risk run by any given individual
a rate per hundred thousand people ignores the size of a country, whereas an absolute figure takes it into account
questions.explanation: Answer: it is an absolute count, so size inflates it whatever the individual's risk. Why: paragraph 3 says a share 'is an absolute figure, and it will tend to be large for a country that is large', while a rate per hundred thousand 'corrects for size'. Why the others fail: health-system quality and self-reporting are never mentioned, and the last option reverses the passage, which says the RATE corrects for size.

questions.question: Each of the following is stated or implied in the passage EXCEPT that
options: a government should publish only the fall in deaths, since the share of cases might alarm the public needlessly
measuring progress as change helps to sustain the funding and the staff of a programme that can show improvement
measuring burden as level helps to decide which districts and groups should receive the most help
a government that cites only the fall may relax even though a very large number of people remain ill
questions.explanation: Answer: the option saying a government should publish only the fall. The passage argues the opposite: paragraph 4 warns that a government citing only the fall 'may relax', and the last paragraph says honest reporting 'would give both'. The other three are in paragraph 4: progress measures sustain effort, burden measures guide resources, and citing only the fall risks complacency. Tip: in EXCEPT questions, the odd one out often contradicts the author's own recommendation.

questions.question: The last paragraph suggests that
options: the public cannot hold two facts in mind at once, so that one of the two statements ought to be left out of reports
pride in progress and urgency about the burden can be held together, provided the public is shown both facts
pride and urgency are in conflict, and a government must therefore choose between celebrating and warning
the World Health Organization's figures are inconsistent and ought not to be quoted in any report on the disease
questions.explanation: Answer: pride and urgency can coexist if the public sees both facts. Why: the paragraph says 'The two are consistent, and only a public that is shown both will be able to hold on to the first without losing sight of the second.' Why the others fail: the author asks for BOTH facts to be reported, never for one to be hidden; says the statements are 'consistent', not in conflict; and never questions the WHO's figures.

questions.question: The author remarks that 'the next ten per cent will not be as easy as the first' in order to
options: criticise the government for having stopped its programmes as soon as the first ten per cent had been achieved
predict that the fall in deaths will soon be reversed, and that the earlier gains will be entirely lost
warn that continued improvement will grow costlier and is not guaranteed by past success
argue that percentage figures of this kind are always unreliable, whoever may be the body that compiles them
questions.explanation: Answer: to warn that further improvement will be costlier and is not guaranteed. Why: it follows the point that the first reductions are cheap and 'the last ... require finding the hardest cases'. Why the others fail: the passage never says programmes were stopped, never predicts a reversal, and never calls percentage figures unreliable. Tip: when a sentence is an example or a warning inside an argument, ask what point the sentence before it was making.

questions.question: According to Dr. Mahapatra, evacuating people from beyond the expected landfall point is defensible chiefly because
options: forecast tracks are uncertain, and wrongly leaving people in danger costs far more than moving people who were safe
forecasts can now say exactly where a storm will land, so that evacuation of any wider area is purely a matter of caution
unnecessary evacuations help the public to remember warnings better, which makes the next order easier to enforce
beach tourism and water sports are the main source of danger, and their suspension alone would not protect lives
questions.explanation: Answer: tracks are uncertain, and the cost of leaving people in danger is far greater than the cost of moving people unnecessarily. Why: he says forecasts do not tell us exactly where a storm will land, the effects 'reach well beyond' the landfall point, and 'When the costs are that unequal, a sensible authority accepts some unnecessary evacuations.' Why the others fail: he says forecasts do NOT give exact landfall; he warns that too many needless moves cause warning fatigue; and he never says tourism is the main danger.

questions.question: The 'paradox of prevention' described by Dr. Mahapatra is that
options: the more people are evacuated, the more people are likely to be harmed by the storm during the evacuation itself
storms that are forecast with the greatest care are the ones that go on to cause the most damage to the coast
authorities that prepare well are praised for it, which tempts them to prepare less thoroughly the next time
successful preparation makes the outcome look uneventful, which invites the belief that the effort was unnecessary
questions.explanation: Answer: success looks like nothing happened, so people think the effort was unnecessary. Why: he says 'When preparation works, the outcome looks uneventful, and uneventfulness is mistaken for proof that the effort was unnecessary.' Why the others fail: harm during evacuation, damage increasing with careful forecasting, and authorities being praised into complacency are never mentioned. Tip: a 'paradox' is a result that seems to contradict common sense; here, doing the job well makes the job look pointless.

questions.question: Dr. Mahapatra would most likely regard the fact that few lives were lost after a large evacuation as
options: conclusive proof that the evacuation was excessive, since a well-judged order would have moved fewer people
no proof by itself that the evacuation was needless, since preparedness should be judged against the hazard and the reach to the vulnerable
evidence that warning fatigue has been avoided, since the public obeyed the order and suffered no loss
an indication that the forecast was wrong, since a correct forecast always leads to a large number of deaths
questions.explanation: Answer: not proof that the evacuation was needless. Why: in his last answer he says preparedness should not be judged 'by the damage visible afterwards' but by 'whether lives were lost relative to what the hazard could have caused' and whether the vulnerable 'were reached in time'. Why the others fail: 'conclusive proof of excess' is exactly the mistake the paradox of prevention describes; warning fatigue is a separate risk that this fact cannot settle; and a correct forecast does not 'always' mean many deaths.

questions.question: The new chief executive's promise to cut costs sharply without losing a single job was widely seen as an attempt to ________.
options: cross the Rubicon
turn a blind eye
move the goalposts
square the circle
questions.explanation: Answer: 'square the circle' means to attempt something that is impossible, or self-contradictory. Cutting costs sharply while losing no jobs is that kind of contradiction. The others: 'cross the Rubicon' means to take a step that cannot be undone; 'turn a blind eye' means to pretend not to notice something; 'move the goalposts' means to change the rules in the middle of a contest.

questions.question: The minister's ________ remarks, delivered with studied indifference, belied the anxiety that his aides privately described.
options: vehement
pensive
nonchalant
guileless
questions.explanation: Answer: 'nonchalant' means casually unconcerned, which fits 'studied indifference'. 'Belied' means contradicted or gave a false impression of, so the remarks looked calm while he was anxious. The others: 'vehement' (forceful) contradicts indifference; 'pensive' (deeply thoughtful) does not suggest indifference; 'guileless' (innocent, without deceit) clashes with the word 'studied', which suggests a deliberate act.

questions.question: Having been ________ by years of unkept promises, the villagers greeted the new scheme with polite scepticism.
options: jaded
galvanised
mollified
gratified
questions.explanation: Answer: 'jaded' means worn out in enthusiasm after long experience of disappointment, which explains their scepticism. The others: 'galvanised' (stirred into action), 'mollified' (calmed down) and 'gratified' (pleased) all describe positive or calming reactions that do not lead to scepticism. Tip: the phrase 'years of unkept promises' tells you the effect on the villagers was negative.

questions.question: The economy looks ________ on the surface, yet its growth is so ________ that a shock to a single sector could prove ________.
options: buoyant; broad; ruinous
sluggish; narrow; ruinous
buoyant; narrow; negligible
buoyant; narrow; ruinous
questions.explanation: Answer: buoyant; narrow; ruinous. Step by step. 'Yet' signals contrast: the economy LOOKS good (buoyant, meaning cheerful and growing), but something underneath is weak. Growth concentrated in few sectors is 'narrow', so a shock to one sector could be 'ruinous' (disastrous). 'Broad' growth would not make a single-sector shock ruinous; 'sluggish' would not need 'yet' because there would be no contrast; 'negligible' contradicts the worry in the sentence.

questions.question: Critics called the scheme ________: its benefits were ________ to a few, while its costs were ________ across the many.
options: regressive; confined; diffused
progressive; confined; diffused
regressive; diffused; confined
progressive; diffused; confined
questions.explanation: Answer: regressive; confined; diffused. Step by step. A 'regressive' scheme burdens the many and favours the few (a progressive one does the reverse). Benefits 'confined' to a few and costs 'diffused' (spread widely) across the many describes exactly that. The pairs with 'progressive' contradict the criticism. The pair 'diffused; confined' reverses the benefits and costs, making the scheme help the many at the cost of the few, which would not be a criticism.

questions.question: Though the evidence was ________, the committee, anxious to avoid giving offence, chose to ________ its findings and ________ any firm recommendation.
options: damning; sharpen; withhold
damning; soften; withhold
inconclusive; soften; withhold
damning; soften; announce
questions.explanation: Answer: damning; soften; withhold. Step by step. 'Though' signals contrast: strong ('damning', meaning severely incriminating) evidence, yet the committee backed away. Anxious to avoid offence, it would 'soften' (not sharpen) its findings and 'withhold' (not announce) a firm recommendation. 'Inconclusive' would remove the contrast that 'though' requires, since weak evidence would naturally lead to a mild report.

questions.question: Far from ________ the shortage, the new rationing rules only ________ it, since hoarding rose sharply.
options: aggravating; mitigated
mitigating; mitigated
mitigating; aggravated
aggravating; aggravated
questions.explanation: Answer: mitigating; aggravated. Step by step. Hoarding rose sharply, so the shortage got WORSE: the rules 'aggravated' it. 'Far from X, only Y' needs Y to be the opposite of X, so X must be 'mitigating' (easing). 'Aggravating; aggravated' gives no contrast, and the pairs that end in 'mitigated' contradict the fact that hoarding rose. Tip: 'mitigate' = make less severe; 'aggravate' = make worse.

questions.question: A judge must be ________, having no personal stake in the outcome, but never ________ in the case before him.
options: disinterested; uninterested
uninterested; disinterested
disinterested; disinterested
uninterested; uninterested
questions.explanation: Answer: disinterested; uninterested. Step by step. 'Disinterested' means impartial, with no personal stake, which is what 'no personal stake' describes. 'Uninterested' means bored or not caring, which is what a judge must never be. The reversed pair would say a judge should be bored and never impartial. The pairs with the same word twice cannot work, since the sentence contrasts the two qualities. Tip: dis-interested = fair; un-interested = indifferent.

questions.question: The speaker agreed to ________ the usual notice period, and the bill, despite loud ________ from a few members, received the President's ________ within a week.
options: wave; descent; ascent
waive; descent; assent
waive; dissent; assent
wave; dissent; ascent
questions.explanation: Answer: waive; dissent; assent. Three homophone pairs. WAIVE = give up a requirement (waive the notice period); WAVE = move the hand or a flowing line of water. DISSENT = disagreement; DESCENT = a going down. ASSENT = formal approval (the President's assent); ASCENT = a climb upward. Each correct word is fixed by the meaning: you waive a rule, members dissent, and the President gives assent. Memory trick: assent and approve both begin with 'a-s/a-p'; ascent has a 'c' like 'climb'.

questions.question: One of the statements below contains a word used incorrectly or inappropriately. Choose the option which has the incorrect or inappropriate usage of the word.
options: The tenants withheld their rent until the repairs were made.
The central tenant of the policy is that growth must be shared by all.
The lawyer cited an earlier ruling in support of her argument.
The site of the new airport was chosen after a long survey.
questions.explanation: Answer: the sentence with 'central tenant'. A 'tenet' is a principle or belief held by a group, so it should read 'central tenet'. A 'tenant' is a person who rents a property, which is correctly used in the first of the other sentences. 'Cited' (quoted as authority) and 'site' (a place) are also correct. Memory trick: tenet has two e's like 'belief'; tenant has 'ant' for the person living in the flat.

questions.question: One of the statements below contains a word used incorrectly or inappropriately. Choose the option which has the incorrect or inappropriate usage of the word.
options: The lorry remained stationary at the crossing for an hour.
The dessert was served only after the main course had been cleared.
The committee's report was a model of brevity and clarity.
The clerk ordered fresh stationary, including pens, ledgers and envelopes.
questions.explanation: Answer: the sentence with 'fresh stationary'. 'Stationery' (with an 'e') means writing materials such as pens and paper; 'stationary' (with an 'a') means not moving. So the lorry sentence is correct. 'Dessert' (the sweet course, two s's) is correctly used, as is 'brevity'. Memory trick: stationEry = envElopes; stationAry = stAying in one place.

questions.question: One of the statements below contains a word used incorrectly or inappropriately. Choose the option which has the incorrect or inappropriate usage of the word.
options: The city council approved the revised budget on Friday.
The defendant was advised by counsel not to comment.
The minister sought the council of senior jurists before drafting the bill.
The audience listened in rapt silence to the speaker.
questions.explanation: Answer: the sentence with 'sought the council of senior jurists'. 'Counsel' means advice (or a lawyer), so the minister should have sought their 'counsel'. A 'council' is a group of people who govern or advise, as in 'city council'. 'Counsel' is correct in the defendant sentence, and 'rapt' (completely absorbed) is correct in the last one. Memory trick: counsel = advice, as in 'counsellor'; council = a committee that meets.

questions.question: No sooner had the minister reached the venue <u>when</u> the protest began.
options: then
than
that
as
questions.explanation: Answer: 'than'. Rule: 'No sooner' is always followed by 'than' (No sooner had he arrived than it began to rain), while 'hardly' and 'scarcely' go with 'when' (Hardly had he arrived when it began to rain). 'No sooner' also takes inversion: 'had + subject + past participle'. 'Then', 'that' and 'as' do not complete this fixed pattern. Memory trick: sooner/than are both comparisons, so 'than' completes the comparison.

questions.question: Having studied the evidence for months, <u>the verdict seemed unjust to the judges</u>.
options: the verdict appeared unjust to them
an unjust verdict was what the judges thought
the unjust verdict was found by the judges
the judges found the verdict unjust
questions.explanation: Answer: 'the judges found the verdict unjust'. Rule: a participle phrase at the start ('Having studied the evidence') must describe the subject of the main clause. Who studied the evidence? The judges, not the verdict. So the judges must be the subject right after the comma. In the other options the subject is 'the verdict', 'an unjust verdict' or 'the unjust verdict', so the opening phrase wrongly seems to describe a verdict (a dangling modifier).

questions.question: He spoke softly lest <u>he woke</u> the sleeping child.
options: he should wake
he would wake
he will wake
he was waking
questions.explanation: Answer: 'he should wake'. Rule: 'lest' means 'for fear that', and it already carries a negative sense, so it is followed by 'should + base verb' (or the bare subjunctive 'he wake'), never by a plain past tense, 'will' or 'would'. Thus 'He spoke softly lest he should wake the child.' Do not add 'not' after lest: 'lest he should not wake' would be a double negative.

questions.question: She is not only brilliant <u>but also works hard</u>.
options: but also a hard worker
but she also works hard
but also hardworking
but also does work hard
questions.explanation: Answer: 'but also hardworking'. Rule: with 'not only ... but also', the two parts must be grammatically parallel. 'Brilliant' is an adjective, so what follows 'but also' must also be an adjective: 'hardworking'. 'A hard worker' is a noun phrase, 'she also works hard' and 'does work hard' are full verb clauses. Quick test: delete 'not only' and 'but also' and see whether the two items can stand side by side: 'brilliant, hardworking'.

questions.question:
Complete the paragraph logically:

A test that is 95 per cent accurate sounds reliable. ____________________. If the condition affects one person in a thousand, most positive results will still be false alarms.
options: But accuracy alone does not say how often a positive result is correct; that depends also on how rare the condition is.
A test of that kind is therefore wrong ninety-five times out of a hundred whenever it reports a positive result.
Rare conditions are never worth testing for, since the results of any test for them will always be unreliable.
Because the test is accurate, its positive results can be trusted whatever the number of people who have the condition.
questions.explanation: Answer: the option that accuracy alone does not say how often a positive is correct, because that also depends on how rare the condition is. Why: the sentence after the blank gives the example of a rare condition producing mostly false alarms. So the blank must introduce the idea that rarity matters. Why the others fail: 'wrong ninety-five times out of a hundred' is false; 'never worth testing' is an extreme claim the passage does not make; 'can be trusted whatever the number' is the opposite of the example. Tip: the blank must set up the example that follows.

questions.question:
Complete the paragraph logically:

Projects are rarely abandoned when they should be. ____________________. Having spent years and large sums on a dam or a metro line, planners feel that stopping would turn the money already spent into waste, though that money is gone whichever way they decide.
options: Planners abandon projects too readily, because the costs already incurred always exceed the benefits that are still to come.
Past spending is the best guide to the future value of a project, and so it should weigh most heavily in the decision.
Large projects are seldom abandoned because they are always worth completing, no matter what they have cost so far.
The reluctance comes from treating past costs as a reason to continue, when only future costs and benefits ought to count.
questions.explanation: Answer: the option about treating past costs as a reason to continue. Why: the next sentence describes planners who feel stopping would 'waste' money already spent, 'though that money is gone whichever way they decide'. That is the sunk-cost fallacy: only future costs and benefits matter. Why the others fail: 'abandon too readily' contradicts the first sentence; 'past spending ... should weigh most' endorses the very error the passage criticises; 'always worth completing' contradicts 'when they should be'.

questions.question:
Complete the paragraph logically:

A notification costs its sender almost nothing and costs its receiver a moment of attention. ____________________. Multiplied across hundreds of senders, those moments add up to a tax on attention that no one voted for.
options: Receivers therefore prize notifications highly, since each one is a gift that costs them nothing to accept.
The sender therefore has little reason to economise, because the cost of the interruption falls entirely on someone else.
Senders therefore bear the full cost of every interruption, and so they send only those messages that matter.
Attention is a resource that cannot be wasted, and so no number of messages could ever harm a receiver.
questions.explanation: Answer: the sender has little reason to economise because the cost falls on someone else. Why: the blank must connect 'costs its sender almost nothing' to the final sentence about a 'tax on attention' that many senders impose together. If the cost is borne by receivers, senders have no incentive to hold back (an externality). Why the others fail: receivers do not 'prize' notifications, since the passage calls the effect a tax; 'senders bear the full cost' contradicts the first sentence; and the last option contradicts the idea that attention is being drained.

questions.question:
Rearrange the five sentences (1-5) into a logical sequence (Type the 5-digit sequence as answer):

1. A firm that hands such work to a machine saves money this year but may find that it has stopped producing the seniors it will need in ten.
2. Every skilled engineer was once a beginner who was given dull work to do.
3. The saving belongs to the firm; the shortage, if it comes, will belong to the whole industry.
4. Generative AI now performs much of that routine work faster and more cheaply than a fresher can.
5. Routine testing, simple bug fixes and first drafts of reports gave juniors the practice from which judgement grows.
questions.explanation: Answer: 2-5-4-1-3. Step by step. Sentence 2 is the opener: it introduces the idea of a beginner given dull work and needs no earlier sentence. Sentence 5 names that 'dull work' (routine testing, bug fixes) and says what it gave juniors. Sentence 4 says 'that routine work', which refers to the routine work in 5. Sentence 1 says 'such work' (the routine work now done by machines) and states the cost to a firm. Sentence 3 begins 'The saving', which refers to the money saved in 1, and closes the argument. Tip: 'that', 'such' and 'the saving' are pointers back to something already named.

questions.question:
Rearrange the five sentences (1-5) into a logical sequence (Type the 5-digit sequence as answer):

1. What matters is how the new duty compares with the duties paid by rival exporters selling the same goods.
2. Such a margin, however, is measured against a tariff structure, and if that structure is itself struck down or rewritten, the margin can vanish overnight.
3. This is why negotiators may rationally delay signing until the structure is clear, even when most of the text has been agreed.
4. A tariff cut is worth little to an exporter in isolation.
5. A margin of preference over rivals, therefore, is the real prize of a trade deal.
questions.explanation: Answer: 4-1-5-2-3. Step by step. Sentence 4 states the starting claim (a cut alone is worth little). Sentence 1 explains what does matter: comparison with rivals' duties. Sentence 5 begins 'therefore' and draws the conclusion: the real prize is a margin over rivals. Sentence 2 begins 'Such a margin, however', which needs the margin to have been named in 5, and adds a complication. Sentence 3 begins 'This is why', explaining a consequence of that complication (delay in signing). Tip: 'however' introduces a problem with what came before; 'This is why' introduces a result.

questions.question:
Rearrange the four sentences (1-4) into a logical sequence (Type the 4-digit sequence as answer):

1. Both are true, and they measure different things: the direction of travel, and the distance still to cover.
2. The first: deaths have fallen by 38 per cent since 2015, faster than the global rate.
3. Consider two statements about India's tuberculosis record.
4. The second: India still accounts for nearly a quarter of the world's cases.
questions.explanation: Answer: 3-2-4-1. Step by step. Sentence 3 introduces 'two statements' and so must come first. Sentences 2 and 4 are those two statements, and 'The first' must precede 'The second', so 2 comes before 4. Sentence 1 begins 'Both are true', which refers to both statements and so must come after them, as the conclusion. Tip: ordinal words (first, second) and words like 'both' fix the order almost automatically.

questions.question:
Rearrange the five sentences (1-5) into a logical sequence (Type the 5-digit sequence as answer):

1. Some benefits reach people who should not receive them, as when one household is counted twice.
2. A good system is therefore judged not by one error rate but by how it balances both.
3. Others fail to reach people who should, as when a genuine claimant is rejected for want of a matching record.
4. Welfare schemes go wrong in two opposite ways.
5. Tightening verification reduces the first error but tends to increase the second.
questions.explanation: Answer: 4-1-3-5-2. Step by step. Sentence 4 states the overall claim (two opposite ways of going wrong). Sentence 1 begins 'Some benefits', giving the first way. Sentence 3 begins 'Others', which only makes sense after 'Some', giving the second way. Sentence 5 refers to 'the first error' and 'the second', so it must follow both. Sentence 2 begins 'therefore' and 'both', and draws the final conclusion. Tip: pairs such as 'some ... others' and 'the first ... the second' fix the order.

questions.question:
Rearrange the five sentences (1-5) into a logical sequence (Type the 5-digit sequence as answer):

1. In a large economy, however, buyers and sellers are strangers, and acquaintance cannot carry the weight.
2. They allow a stranger's promise to be relied upon without anyone having to know the stranger.
3. A shopkeeper in a small town needs no contract to sell on credit to a neighbour.
4. Trust comes cheaply among people who know one another.
5. Institutions such as courts, credit agencies and regulators are the substitutes that societies invent.
questions.explanation: Answer: 4-3-1-5-2. Step by step. Sentence 4 states the general idea (trust is cheap among acquaintances). Sentence 3 is an example of it (the small-town shopkeeper). Sentence 1 begins 'In a large economy, however', contrasting with the small-town case. Sentence 5 introduces institutions as 'substitutes' for acquaintance, which only makes sense after the problem in 1. Sentence 2 begins 'They', which refers to the institutions in 5. Tip: 'however' marks a turn in the argument, and a bare 'They' must have a plural noun just before it.

title: IPMAT Indore VA Sectional – 23rd Nov 2026 (Advanced Analytical – High Difficulty)

passages.RC1:
Every November, Delhi's air produces a ritual of blame, and in the ritual the blame usually has a single address: the farm fires of Punjab and Haryana. Satellites that count the fires and models that estimate their smoke do show a seasonal surge, so the habit is not baseless. But this year the script has been awkward to follow. Farm fires in Punjab between 15 September and 1 November numbered 1,514, against 2,084 in the corresponding period a year earlier, and on 31 October stubble contributed a mere 1.6 per cent of the city's fine particulate matter. Yet within days the air quality index stood at 389, the second stage of the Graded Response Action Plan had been imposed, and by mid-month the third stage was in force. Fewer fires and a worse smog appear to contradict one another.

They do so only if one confuses a contribution with a cause. The concentration of pollutants over a city depends on two things: how much is emitted, and how readily the air carries it away. In November the second factor collapses. Cold air settles near the ground under a warmer layer, winds drop, and whatever is emitted stays where it is. The same quantity of smoke that disappears in July therefore hangs over the city in winter. A pollution episode is thus a joint product of emissions and weather, and a fall in one of the two inputs can be more than cancelled by a deterioration in the other.

This is why the question of what adds to the pollution must be kept apart from the question of what turns an addition into a danger. Stubble is a partial answer to the first question for a few weeks each year; meteorology answers the second. Delhi's own emissions from traffic, dust, industry and the burning of waste are present every day, and they form a base on which the episodic contributions are stacked. Their relative size is visible in the data: on one early-November day the official decision-support system put transport at 15.8 per cent and stubble at 15.3 per cent, so that the two were of nearly equal weight. Stubble is an episodic contributor to a chronic problem, and a chronic problem cannot be explained by an episode.

Averages can also mislead in the other direction. A source that contributes fifteen per cent on average may be decisive on the day when the air is already close to a threshold, because the index is a banded scale and policy is tied to the bands. Think of a glass that is nearly full: the last drop is not the reason for the overflow, yet removing it would have prevented the overflow that day, and removing it would do nothing for the next day, when the glass is filled again. The marginal contribution of a source on a bad day can thus be far larger than its share over the season. Those who wish to blame neighbouring states quote the peaks; those who wish to defend farmers quote the averages. Each side selects the statistic that suits a conclusion reached in advance.

The stages of the action plan are themselves triggered by the index, which is an outcome, and not by the source of the pollution. They restrict construction, diesel generators and certain vehicles, which are the things that lie within the city's control, and they are lifted when the index improves. They are therefore a way of managing the peak, not of lowering the base. A serious policy would separate three things: the base of year-round local emissions, the episodic additions such as stubble and firecrackers, and the weather that amplifies both. Only the first two can be controlled, and the first is the larger prize, since it is present on every day, including those on which nobody is watching the index. To quarrel over the share of one source on one day is to quarrel about the last drop.
passages.RC2:
The phrase 'first made-in-India chip' has been promised so often in recent years that its arrival, in whatever form, tends to be received as an event. As of mid-2026 the government has approved twelve semiconductor projects worth about ₹1.64 lakh crore, and in February Micron's plant at Sanand was inaugurated, handing its first memory modules to Dell. The milestone is real. But a milestone names a moment, not a position. The journey from silicon to device has stages whose economics differ enormously, and being present at one of them says little about being present at the others.

Consider the three stages. Design, the first, creates the blueprint of a chip, and it rewards intellectual property and talent with the highest margins and the least equipment. Fabrication, the middle stage, turns wafers into working circuits; it is the most capital-intensive, demanding plants that cost billions, ultra-pure water, unbroken power and a dense network of suppliers of materials and tools. Packaging, the last, cuts the finished wafers, encloses the chips and tests them; it needs far less capital and is far quicker to build. A country can therefore enter at the packaging end fast, producing output and jobs within a couple of years, while fabrication takes many years to mature. The price of the quick entry is a smaller share of the value: the wafers are generally imported, and so are the designs, and what remains for the packaging plant is the thinner margin of the last step.

Why enter at all, given the sums involved? The commercial argument is weak. Chips can usually be bought more cheaply from established producers, and the subsidy per job created is large. The strategic argument is stronger. Fabrication is concentrated in a very few places, and a country that has no capacity of its own is at the mercy of any disruption to them, whether by accident, by conflict or by policy. Seen in this light, the subsidy is better understood as an insurance premium than as an investment with a return. Its benefit lies in the disruption that does not happen, and a disruption that never happens is never seen, which is why the spending is so easily criticised in normal years. Insurance, however, works only if the cover is adequate to the risk. A small capacity in the wrong kind of chip protects against very little.

It is for this reason that the widening of the mission deserves attention. The second phase, announced this year, is reported to extend support beyond plants to design, equipment, research and talent. The logic is that of complementarity: a plant surrounded by suppliers, designers and trained engineers is worth more than the same plant standing alone, because each of these raises the value of the others. The first phase was occupied with getting plants approved and built. The second must build their neighbourhood. There is also a risk to be watched. Subsidies attract those investors who need them most, and a plant that exists only because of the subsidy may leave when the subsidy ends, taking its equipment and its know-how with it.

Judging the mission by the date of the first chip therefore directs attention to the wrong thing. Better tests are available: what share of the value of the final product is retained in India, how many suppliers are domestic, whether Indian design firms have begun to use Indian plants, and whether any plant would stay if the support were withdrawn. By these tests the mission is at an early stage. That is not a failure, but nor is it yet a success; it is a beginning, and it should be called one.
passages.RC3:
A payment that arrives in seconds has an unwelcome property: it also leaves in seconds. The instant systems, UPI and IMPS among them, that have made India's digital payments some of the most widely used in the world were designed to remove delay, and delay was what, in older systems, gave a bank time to notice a fraud and stop it. The Reserve Bank of India observed in a discussion paper released in April that a typical fraud in this setting may involve no breach of technical systems at all; it works through the manipulation of users, by social engineering, coercion or impersonation. Parliament was told in December that UPI frauds up to November of the last financial year were worth ₹805 crore across 10.64 lakh incidents. In many of these cases the customer has not been robbed in the ordinary sense. She has herself authorised the payment, believing it to be genuine. The regulators call this authorised push payment fraud.

That is what makes it hard to cure by the usual means. Stronger authentication, such as two-factor checks or the binding of an account to a device, establishes that the person sending the money is the account holder. In authorised fraud that check passes, because it is the account holder who is sending the money. The security is working perfectly, and the fraud succeeds. The weakness lies not in the lock but in the person holding the key, and what would help is not a better lock but something that interrupts that person's decision at the moment it is made.

Hence the measures the central bank is reported to be weighing: a short delay, perhaps an hour, on certain payments; wider controls in the hands of customers; and a mechanism to freeze a transfer that is suspected. What they have in common is that they add friction deliberately. Friction is ordinarily thought of as a defect to be engineered away, but here it is the product. A scammer's chief weapon is urgency. The message says that the account will be blocked within the hour, or that the arrest will follow within minutes, and the victim, hurried, does not stop to ask anyone. A pause gives the deceived time to consult a relative, to call the bank, to notice that the demand does not quite make sense. Time is the scammer's enemy.

Friction, however, is not free, and its costs fall unevenly. A delay on every payment would tax the many honest users who pay a vegetable seller, or a hospital in an emergency, in order to protect the few who would otherwise be deceived. The obvious reply is to target it: to hold only the payments that look unusual, such as a first transfer to a new payee, a large sum, or an odd hour. Targeting lowers the cost, but it depends on a model of what is unusual, and the model will err in both directions, holding honest payments and missing dishonest ones. Fraudsters, moreover, adapt. If large transfers are held, they ask for several small ones.

There remains the question of who bears the loss when fraud succeeds. Where a bank must bear part of it, the bank has a reason to build better detection; where the whole of it falls on the customer, the reason is weaker. Rules that spread some of the loss to banks and payment providers are therefore not merely a matter of compensation but a part of the design. The problem is at bottom one of allocation. Someone must pay for the delay, in time or in money, and the real choice lies between many small costs borne by all users and a few large costs borne by victims.
passages.CA1:
CONVERSATION ANALYSIS: Read the following transcript and choose the answer that is closest to each of the questions that are based on the transcript.

Rohan Mehta (Host, Business Desk): Tomato prices have doubled in several cities within a fortnight, and food inflation is leading the headlines. Shouldn't the central bank raise interest rates to cool this?

Prof. Anjali Deshpande (agricultural economist): Only if raising rates would bring back the tomatoes. A rate increase works by dampening demand across the economy. This spike comes from supply: heavy rain damaged the crop and disrupted transport. Cooling the demand for cars and homes will not grow a single tomato. A sensible central bank looks through a shock that is likely to reverse, and acts only if it begins to change what people expect about future prices.

Rohan Mehta: Why would it reverse?

Prof. Deshpande: Because vegetables are perishable and supply responds quickly. Farmers who see high prices plant more, and the new crop arrives in weeks, not years. Such prices swing sharply in both directions, which is why they make the headline figure jumpy while the core figure, which leaves out food and fuel, stays steadier.

Rohan Mehta: But a household cannot eat the core figure.

Prof. Deshpande: Quite right, and that is the second half of the answer. The central bank has the wrong tool, but the problem is real, especially for poorer families, who spend a larger share of their income on food. The useful responses are on the supply side: storage and transport that smooth a local glut or shortage, and information that stops farmers from planting in a herd. There is a further puzzle. When consumers pay double, farmers rarely receive double. Much of the increase is captured in the middle, by transport, wholesale and retail margins.

Rohan Mehta: So who gains?

Prof. Deshpande: Often neither the farmer nor the consumer.

questions.question: Which of the following best states the central argument of the passage?
options: Stubble burning in Punjab and Haryana is no longer a significant source of Delhi's pollution, and the neighbouring states should be absolved of all blame
Delhi's air quality index is an unreliable measure of pollution, and that is why the stages of the action plan are triggered at the wrong times
Weather is the only real cause of Delhi's winter smog, since the emissions of the city remain exactly the same throughout the whole year
Delhi's smog comes from a chronic base of local emissions, episodic additions and winter weather, so blaming one source misreads the problem and misdirects policy
questions.explanation: Answer: the smog has three parts (base emissions, episodic additions, weather), so blaming one source misdirects policy. Why: paragraph 2 says an episode is a 'joint product of emissions and weather'; paragraph 3 separates the year-round base from episodic additions; the last paragraph names 'three things' to be separated. Why the others fail: the author never says stubble is insignificant, only that it is one contributor (paragraph 3 gives it a share of about 15 per cent); the index is never called unreliable, it is called an outcome; and 'weather is the only cause' contradicts the 'joint product' idea. Tip: main-idea answers must cover the whole passage, and extreme words such as 'only' and 'no longer' are red flags.

questions.question: The passage says that fewer farm fires and a worse smog 'appear to contradict one another' but do so 'only if one confuses a contribution with a cause'. This is because
options: the satellites that count the fires are known to understate the number of fires in Punjab, so the official count of fires is unreliable
the concentration of pollutants depends on how much is emitted and also on how readily the air disperses it, and winter conditions reduce the latter
the restrictions under the action plan themselves add to emissions during the first few days after they have been imposed on the city
the smoke from farm fires travels more slowly in winter than in other seasons, and so reaches the city only after a long delay
questions.explanation: Answer: pollution depends on emissions AND dispersal, and winter reduces dispersal. Why: paragraph 2 says 'The concentration of pollutants over a city depends on two things: how much is emitted, and how readily the air carries it away', and in November 'the second factor collapses' (cold air near the ground, low winds). So a fall in one input (fires) can be more than cancelled by a worse second input (weather). Why the others fail: no unreliability of satellites, no extra emissions from the action plan, and no slower travel of smoke is mentioned. Tip: when a passage says two facts 'seem to contradict', the answer is usually a hidden third factor.

questions.question: The image of the nearly full glass in the fourth paragraph implies that
options: a source with a modest average share can still decide whether a threshold is crossed on a particular day
the source that contributes least to the pollution should be the first one to be dealt with by policy
removing a single source would permanently prevent every episode of smog in the city in later years
an average taken over a whole season is a more reliable guide than the reading on any single bad day
questions.explanation: Answer: a modest-share source can decide whether a threshold is crossed on a given day. How to decode the image: the glass is the air near its limit, the last drop is a source with a small share. Removing it prevents the overflow that day (the marginal effect), but the glass is filled again next day, so the base still matters. The text confirms: 'The marginal contribution of a source on a bad day can thus be far larger than its share over the season.' Why the others fail: the image does not rank sources for policy, does not promise a permanent cure (the glass fills again), and the passage says averages can mislead. Tip: translate every metaphor into plain words, then check the options.

questions.question: The author's attitude to those who blame neighbouring states and those who defend farmers is best described as
options: approving, because each side quotes figures that are accurate and thereby helps the public to see the whole picture
indifferent, because the peaks and the averages in any case lead to the same conclusion about whom to blame
critical, because each side selects the statistic that suits a conclusion it had reached in advance
alarmed, because both sides are said in the passage to have altered the data that they present to the public
questions.explanation: Answer: critical, because each side picks a statistic to fit a conclusion decided in advance. Why: paragraph 4 says 'Those who wish to blame neighbouring states quote the peaks; those who wish to defend farmers quote the averages. Each side selects the statistic that suits a conclusion reached in advance.' Why the others fail: the author does not approve (selecting a number to fit a conclusion is a fault), the peaks and averages do NOT lead to the same conclusion, and no one is accused of altering data, only of selecting it.

questions.question: Each of the following is stated or implied in the passage EXCEPT that
options: on one early-November day transport and stubble burning had nearly equal shares in the city's pollution
farm fires in Punjab rose this year compared with the corresponding period of the previous year
winter weather lets pollutants stay where they are emitted, since cold air settles and the winds drop
the stages of the action plan are triggered by the index and not by the source of the pollution
questions.explanation: Answer: the option saying farm fires rose. Paragraph 1 says the opposite: 1,514 fires against 2,084 a year earlier, so they FELL. The others are in the text: paragraph 3 (transport 15.8 per cent, stubble 15.3 per cent), paragraph 2 (cold air settles near the ground and winds drop) and paragraph 5 (the stages are triggered by the index, 'an outcome'). Tip: in EXCEPT questions, the odd one out is often the direct reverse of a number or fact in the text, so recheck the figures.

questions.question: Which of the following policies would the author most likely endorse?
options: Lifting the restrictions of the action plan earlier, since they are costly and bring relief only at the peaks
Concentrating policy on stubble burning, since it is the only source that lies outside the city's control
Waiting for the weather to improve, since the emissions themselves cannot be controlled by any authority
Lowering the year-round local emissions, since they form a base that is present even when nobody is watching the index
questions.explanation: Answer: lowering the year-round local emissions. Why: the last paragraph says the base of local emissions is 'the larger prize, since it is present on every day, including those on which nobody is watching the index'. Why the others fail: the author does not ask for restrictions to be lifted (they manage the peak, which is still useful); the passage never says stubble is the ONLY source outside the city's control, and the author calls it episodic; and the author says the base and the episodic additions CAN be controlled, only the weather cannot.

questions.question: Which of the following best states the main point of the passage?
options: India's semiconductor mission has failed, since the plants that have been approved capture only the thinnest part of the value of a chip
The strategic case for subsidising chips is weak, and the money would be better spent on buying chips from established producers
A first chip is a milestone and not proof of position; the mission should be judged by the value and ecosystem India retains, and by these tests it is still at a beginning
Chip design is the only stage worth entering, and the mission should therefore give up fabrication and packaging altogether
questions.explanation: Answer: a first chip is only a milestone; judge the mission by value and ecosystem retained; by those tests it is a beginning. Why: paragraph 1 says 'a milestone names a moment, not a position', and the last paragraph ends 'it is a beginning'. Why the others fail: the author says 'That is not a failure'; the strategic case is called 'stronger' than the commercial one, so it is not weak; and the author never says design is the only stage worth entering.

questions.question: The statement that 'a milestone names a moment, not a position' means that
options: reaching a single event, such as a first shipment, does not show where a country stands in the whole chain of chip-making
the dates of milestones are often announced wrongly by officials, so that the progress of the mission cannot be measured
a country can take a position in the chain only after it has passed all of the milestones that have been set for it
milestones matter only to the officials who announce them, and not to the industry that is supposed to benefit from them
questions.explanation: Answer: one event does not show where a country stands in the whole chain. Decode: a 'moment' is a single event (the first memory modules to Dell); a 'position' is where one stands across design, fabrication and packaging. The next sentence says so: 'being present at one of them says little about being present at the others.' Why the others fail: the passage does not say that officials announce dates wrongly, does not tie positions to passing milestones, and never says that milestones matter only to officials.

questions.question: According to the passage, entry at the packaging end is quicker but yields a smaller share of the value because
options: packaging demands more skilled engineers than fabrication does, and such engineers take several years to be trained
packaging plants are barred from selling their output to the firms that have designed the chips they are packaging
the chips that come from packaging plants are of lower quality than those that come from fabrication plants
packaging needs less capital and builds quickly, but works on wafers and designs that are mostly imported, which leaves the thinner margin of the last step
questions.explanation: Answer: packaging needs less capital and is quick to build, but it works on imported wafers and designs, so it keeps only the thin margin of the last step. Why: paragraph 2 says 'The price of the quick entry is a smaller share of the value: the wafers are generally imported, and so are the designs.' Why the others fail: the passage never mentions engineers' skills, legal bars on selling, or lower quality of packaged chips.

questions.question: Each of the following is stated or implied in the passage EXCEPT that
options: design earns the highest margins and needs the least equipment of the three stages
fabrication needs less capital than packaging, which is why the first phase began with the building of fabrication plants
fabrication depends on a dense network of suppliers of materials and tools
a plant that exists only because of a subsidy may leave when the subsidy ends
questions.explanation: Answer: the option saying fabrication needs less capital than packaging. Paragraph 2 says fabrication is 'the most capital-intensive' stage and packaging 'needs far less capital'. The passage also says the first phase was occupied with getting plants approved and built, and does not say it began with fabrication. The other three are stated: paragraph 2 (design margins, suppliers) and paragraph 4 (a subsidised plant may leave). Tip: look for options that reverse a comparison.

questions.question: The comparison of the subsidy to an insurance premium implies that
options: its value lies in the risk it removes, which stays invisible in normal years, and it counts only if the cover is adequate
subsidies should be judged by the profit that the plants make in each normal year after they have begun production
any amount of capacity, however small, gives full protection against a disruption of the supply of chips
the spending is justified only if an actual disruption of supply takes place within the next few years
questions.explanation: Answer: the value lies in the risk removed (invisible in normal years), and it counts only if the cover is adequate. Why: paragraph 3 says 'a disruption that never happens is never seen' and 'A small capacity in the wrong kind of chip protects against very little.' Why the others fail: judging by yearly profit misses the point of insurance; the passage says small capacity protects against 'very little', so it does not give full protection; and an insurance premium is not justified only by a disaster actually occurring.

questions.question: Which of the following would the author regard as the best sign that the mission is succeeding?
options: The announcement by a minister that the first chip will be produced before the end of the current year
A rise in the number of projects approved under the mission and in the total sum that has been committed
A plant that stays and expands after support is withdrawn, together with growing use of it by Indian design firms
A rise in the size of the subsidy that is paid for each plant, so that more investors are attracted to it
questions.explanation: Answer: a plant that stays and expands without support, and use of it by Indian design firms. Why: the last paragraph lists the tests: value retained, domestic suppliers, whether Indian design firms use Indian plants, 'and whether any plant would stay if the support were withdrawn'. Why the others fail: the author says judging by the date of the first chip 'directs attention to the wrong thing'; approvals and sums committed are inputs, not results; and a larger subsidy attracts the very investors who 'need it most', which the author treats as a risk.

questions.question: Which of the following best states the central argument of the passage?
options: Digital payment fraud in India is rising so fast that the instant payment systems should now be abandoned in favour of slower ones
Because authorised fraud passes every authentication check, regulators are weighing deliberate friction, whose costs must be targeted and fairly allocated
Stronger authentication is the best cure for authorised fraud, and the regulators are right to go on strengthening it in every system
Banks should bear the whole of every loss from fraud, since customers cannot be expected to protect themselves in any way
questions.explanation: Answer: authorised fraud passes authentication, so deliberate friction is being weighed, and its cost must be targeted and allocated. Why: paragraph 2 explains why authentication fails; paragraph 3 explains friction; paragraph 4 explains targeting; paragraph 5 says 'The problem is at bottom one of allocation.' Why the others fail: the author never suggests abandoning instant payments; authentication is said NOT to cure this kind of fraud; and banks bearing the 'whole' loss is not argued (the passage says 'part').

questions.question: According to the passage, stronger authentication fails against authorised push payment fraud because
options: the account holder herself approves the payment, so the check that she is the account holder is passed
authentication works only for card payments and does not apply to the instant transfers that are made through UPI
scammers are able to break into the systems of banks and thereby to pass the checks that are meant to stop them
authentication slows payments so much that users prefer to turn it off, and fraud then goes unchecked
questions.explanation: Answer: the account holder herself approves the payment, so the check passes. Why: paragraph 2 says 'In authorised fraud that check passes, because it is the account holder who is sending the money', and compares it to a lock that works while the person holding the key is deceived. Why the others fail: nothing says authentication applies only to cards; paragraph 1 says such fraud 'may involve no breach of technical systems at all'; and users turning it off is not mentioned.

questions.question: The author says that 'time is the scammer's enemy' because
options: a pause allows the bank to trace the physical location of the scammer before the money has been moved
scammers cannot hold the attention of their victims over any long period, and so they lose interest quickly
delays raise the cost of carrying out the fraud, since each scam then needs many more calls and messages
scams depend on urgency, and a pause gives the victim time to reflect or to consult someone else
questions.explanation: Answer: scams depend on urgency, and a pause lets the victim reflect or consult. Why: paragraph 3 says 'A scammer's chief weapon is urgency', gives the examples of 'the account will be blocked within the hour', and says a pause gives time 'to consult a relative, to call the bank, to notice that the demand does not quite make sense'. Why the others fail: tracing the scammer, short attention spans and higher costs of operation are not mentioned.

questions.question: Each of the following is stated or implied in the passage EXCEPT that
options: a delay on every payment would burden honest users, such as those who must pay a hospital in an emergency
a model of what is unusual will make errors in both directions, holding honest payments and missing dishonest ones
once a hold on unusual payments is introduced, it will reduce fraud to a negligible level without any further cost
fraudsters may respond to a hold on large sums by asking their victims to make several small transfers
questions.explanation: Answer: the option claiming a hold will cut fraud to a negligible level at no cost. The passage argues the opposite: 'Friction, however, is not free', targeting depends on a fallible model, and fraudsters adapt. The other three are in paragraph 4: the burden on honest users, the errors in both directions, and the splitting of large transfers into small ones. Tip: options with absolute words such as 'negligible' and 'without any cost' usually go beyond what the author says.

questions.question: The fifth paragraph suggests that
options: rules about compensation are relevant only after a fraud has taken place, and they cannot affect the design of systems
banks bear no loss in any case, since the payment has been authorised by the customer who made it
customers take more care when the whole loss falls on them, so that detection by banks becomes unnecessary
a bank has less reason to build better detection when the whole loss from fraud falls on the customer
questions.explanation: Answer: a bank has less reason to build better detection if the whole loss falls on the customer. Why: paragraph 5 says 'Where a bank must bear part of it, the bank has a reason to build better detection; where the whole of it falls on the customer, the reason is weaker.' It adds that loss-sharing rules are 'a part of the design'. Why the others fail: that contradicts the 'part of the design' line; the paragraph deals with banks sharing loss, so 'no loss in any case' is wrong; and customer care is not claimed to make detection unnecessary.

questions.question: The last sentence of the passage suggests that
options: some cost is unavoidable, and the open question is who should bear it and in what form
a design exists that would remove all cost from both honest users and the victims of fraud
the victims should always bear the cost, since they alone have made the payment in question
honest users should never be inconvenienced, even if the number of frauds were to go on rising
questions.explanation: Answer: some cost is unavoidable; the question is who bears it. Why: the sentence says 'Someone must pay for the delay, in time or in money', and the choice is between 'many small costs borne by all users and a few large costs borne by victims'. Why the others fail: it says a cost must be paid, so a no-cost design does not exist; it does not say victims should always pay; and it does not say honest users must never be inconvenienced.

questions.question: According to Prof. Deshpande, a rise in interest rates is not the right response to the tomato price spike chiefly because
options: interest rates have no effect at all on any kind of inflation, whatever the cause of the rise may be
tomatoes form too small a part of the index for the central bank to take any notice of their price
the spike comes from supply, whereas a rate rise works by dampening demand
the central bank is not permitted by the law to react to changes in the prices of food items
questions.explanation: Answer: the spike comes from supply, while a rate rise works on demand. Why: she says 'A rate increase works by dampening demand across the economy. This spike comes from supply' and 'Cooling the demand for cars and homes will not grow a single tomato.' Why the others fail: she does not say interest rates never work, does not talk about the size of tomatoes in the index, and does not mention any legal bar.

questions.question: Prof. Deshpande says a central bank should act on such a spike only if
options: the spike lasts for more than a fortnight in any one of the cities that are affected by it
it begins to change what people expect about future prices
the core figure rises above the headline figure for two months in a row after the spike
farmers decide to plant more of the crop because of the higher prices they have seen
questions.explanation: Answer: if the spike begins to change what people expect about future prices. Why: she says a sensible central bank 'acts only if it begins to change what people expect about future prices'. Why the others fail: duration in a city, the core figure overtaking the headline figure and farmers planting more are not given as triggers; in fact farmers planting more is her reason why the spike will REVERSE.

questions.question: Prof. Deshpande's last two remarks suggest that
options: the gain from higher retail prices is largely absorbed by intermediaries, so that farmers do not benefit in proportion
farmers gain much more from a sharp rise in prices than consumers lose by paying the higher prices
consumers benefit from price spikes, since farmers then plant more and later prices fall below earlier levels
intermediaries lose heavily when prices rise, because the margins that they are allowed to earn are fixed
questions.explanation: Answer: intermediaries absorb much of the gain, so farmers do not gain in proportion. Why: she says 'When consumers pay double, farmers rarely receive double. Much of the increase is captured in the middle', and to 'who gains?' she answers 'Often neither the farmer nor the consumer.' Why the others fail: each contradicts one of these remarks (farmers gaining more than consumers lose, consumers benefiting, intermediaries losing).

questions.question: An ________ sceptic, she greeted every promise of reform with the same weary doubt.
options: fledgling
ephemeral
inveterate
ingenuous
questions.explanation: Answer: 'inveterate' means long-established in a habit, which fits someone who always meets promises with the same doubt. The others: 'fledgling' means new and inexperienced (the opposite of long-established); 'ephemeral' means short-lived; 'ingenuous' means innocent and trusting, which clashes with 'sceptic'. Tip: 'the same weary doubt' hints at habit built over time.

questions.question: The regulator's ________ reply, neither approving the merger nor rejecting it, left both firms unsure how to proceed.
options: categorical
equivocal
emphatic
unequivocal
questions.explanation: Answer: 'equivocal' means open to more than one interpretation, deliberately unclear. The clue is 'neither approving nor rejecting', which left the firms unsure. The others: 'categorical' (absolute and clear), 'emphatic' (forceful) and 'unequivocal' (leaving no doubt) all describe clear replies, the opposite of what the sentence needs.

questions.question: The new chief's frugality was ________ in a firm accustomed to lavish expense accounts, and it soon became a talking point.
options: unremarkable
negligible
innocuous
conspicuous
questions.explanation: Answer: 'conspicuous' means standing out, easily noticed. A frugal chief in a lavish firm would stand out, and that is why it became a talking point. The others: 'unremarkable' and 'negligible' describe something that does not attract notice, so it could not become a talking point; 'innocuous' means harmless, which does not explain the attention.

questions.question: Although the new scheme was widely ________ as a breakthrough, its ________ was limited, for it reached only a small ________ of those it was meant to help.
options: decried; impact; fraction
touted; impact; fraction
touted; impact; majority
touted; novelty; fraction
questions.explanation: Answer: touted; impact; fraction. Step by step. 'Although' signals contrast: the scheme was praised ('touted') but its effect ('impact') was limited, because it reached only a small 'fraction'. 'Decried' (condemned) would not contrast with 'limited'; 'small majority' does not make sense for a limited reach; and 'novelty' is not made limited by reaching few people.

questions.question: The orator was ________ rather than persuasive: his speech was long on ________ and short on ________.
options: bombastic; rhetoric; substance
bombastic; substance; rhetoric
laconic; rhetoric; substance
lucid; rhetoric; substance
questions.explanation: Answer: bombastic; rhetoric; substance. Step by step. 'Bombastic' means pompous and full of inflated words, the opposite of persuasive. Such a speech is long on 'rhetoric' (fine-sounding language) and short on 'substance' (real content). Reversing the last two would praise the content. 'Laconic' means using few words, which clashes with 'long on'; 'lucid' means clear, which would not be set against 'persuasive' in this way.

questions.question: The treaty's language was deliberately ________: each side could claim victory because each could read into the text a meaning that ________ its own position, and the vagueness would ________ only when the first dispute arose.
options: precise; vindicated; surface
ambiguous; contradicted; surface
ambiguous; vindicated; vanish
ambiguous; vindicated; surface
questions.explanation: Answer: ambiguous; vindicated; surface. Step by step. Both sides claim victory, so the text must be open to two readings ('ambiguous', not 'precise'). Each reads a meaning that 'vindicated' (supported) its own position; a meaning that 'contradicted' it would not let it claim victory. The vagueness would 'surface' (come to the notice) only when a dispute arose; it would not 'vanish' at that point, since a dispute is exactly when the vagueness matters.

questions.question: The auditor was ________ about the accounts, ________ every figure and ________ any entry that could not be traced to a source.
options: cavalier; scrutinising; querying
scrupulous; overlooking; querying
scrupulous; scrutinising; querying
scrupulous; scrutinising; condoning
questions.explanation: Answer: scrupulous; scrutinising; querying. Step by step. A careful auditor is 'scrupulous' (extremely careful about detail); 'cavalier' (careless) is the opposite. Such a person 'scrutinises' (examines closely), not 'overlooks', every figure, and 'queries' (questions) an untraceable entry rather than 'condoning' (accepting or forgiving) it.

questions.question: The study ________ a strong correlation between the two, but it would be ________ to conclude that one causes the other, since both may depend on a third factor.
options: disproved; unwarranted
documented; prudent
documented; unwarranted
documented; inevitable
questions.explanation: Answer: documented; unwarranted. Step by step. 'But' signals a limit on what follows. The study 'documented' (recorded) a correlation, but to claim causation would be 'unwarranted' (without justification) because a third factor may explain both. 'Disproved' a correlation would not need 'but'; 'prudent' (wise) and 'inevitable' (certain) reverse the caution that the sentence expresses.

questions.question: An ________ jurist warned that a constitutional crisis was ________ and urged members to ________ their usual debates.
options: imminent; eminent; forgo
eminent; imminent; forego
eminent; immanent; forgo
eminent; imminent; forgo
questions.explanation: Answer: eminent; imminent; forgo. Three confusable words. EMINENT = distinguished (an eminent jurist); IMMINENT = about to happen (a crisis that is imminent); IMMANENT = inherent, existing within. FORGO = do without, give up; FOREGO = go before, precede. So 'forgo their usual debates' means to give them up. Memory trick: imMINENT sounds like 'MINUTES away'; forGO = let go of something; foreGO = go FORE (before).

questions.question: One of the statements below contains a word used incorrectly or inappropriately. Choose the option which has the incorrect or inappropriate usage of the word.
options: The principle of the college addressed the graduating class.
The principal reason for the delay was a shortage of cement.
She refused to compromise her principles, even under pressure.
The judge based her ruling on a legal precedent.
questions.explanation: Answer: the sentence with 'The principle of the college'. A 'principal' is the head of an institution (and, as an adjective, 'main'); a 'principle' is a rule or belief. So the college has a 'principal'. The other sentences are correct: 'principal reason' (main reason), 'principles' (beliefs) and 'precedent' (an earlier ruling). Memory trick: the princiPAL is your PAL; a principLE is a ruLE.

questions.question: One of the statements below contains a word used incorrectly or inappropriately. Choose the option which has the incorrect or inappropriate usage of the word.
options: The site chosen for the new factory was carefully surveyed.
The lawyer asked the witness to site the exact date of the incident.
The court cited an earlier ruling in support of its view.
The old man was gradually losing his sight.
questions.explanation: Answer: the sentence with 'to site the exact date'. To 'cite' means to mention or quote as evidence, so the witness should 'cite' (name) the date. A 'site' is a place, correctly used in the first of the other options; 'cited' is correctly used in the second; and 'sight' (the ability to see) is correct in the last. Memory trick: CITE = CITation; SITE = a SITuation or place; SIGHT = eyesight.

questions.question: One of the statements below contains a word used incorrectly or inappropriately. Choose the option which has the incorrect or inappropriate usage of the word.
options: The jockey tightened the reins before the start of the race.
Heavy rain delayed the match for nearly two hours.
The new queen's reign began in the spring.
The dictator's rein of terror ended only with his exile.
questions.explanation: Answer: the sentence with 'rein of terror'. A period of rule is a 'reign'. A 'rein' is the strap used to control a horse, correctly used in the jockey sentence; 'rain' is water from the sky, correct in the third; 'reign' is correct in the last. Memory trick: reiGN has a 'g' like 'governor' and 'king'; a reIN is what you hold to steer a horse.

questions.question: Neither the manager nor his assistants <u>was</u> aware of the change.
options: is
has been
were
was being
questions.explanation: Answer: 'were'. Rule: with 'neither ... nor', the verb agrees with the subject NEAREST to it. The nearest subject is 'assistants' (plural), so the verb is 'were'. (If the order were 'Neither his assistants nor the manager', the verb would be singular: 'was'.) 'Is' and 'has been' are singular and present or perfect forms that do not match the past sense; 'was being' is a continuous form that makes no sense with 'aware'.

questions.question: Each of the proposals, along with their costings, <u>have been</u> examined.
options: has been
are being
were
being
questions.explanation: Answer: 'has been'. Rule: 'Each' is singular, so the verb must be singular. The phrase 'along with their costings' is parenthetical and does not change the number of the subject. So 'Each of the proposals ... has been examined.' 'Are being' and 'were' are plural, and 'being' alone leaves the sentence without a finite verb.

questions.question: I wish the committee <u>would have</u> published the report earlier.
options: has published
had published
would publish
will have published
questions.explanation: Answer: 'had published'. Rule: 'wish' about a past event takes the past perfect (I wish he had come). 'Would have' is not used in the clause that follows 'wish' for a past regret. 'Has published' and 'will have published' do not express a wish about the past, and 'would publish' refers to the future.

questions.question: The profits of this year are higher than <u>last year</u>.
options: that of last year
what last year was
those of last year
last year are
questions.explanation: Answer: 'those of last year'. Rule: comparisons must compare like with like. 'Profits' are being compared with 'profits', not with a 'year'. The pronoun 'those' stands for 'profits' (plural). 'That of' would need a singular noun; the other options are ungrammatical. Tip: ask 'what is being compared with what?' and make both sides the same kind of thing.

questions.question:
Complete the paragraph logically:

A survey of train passengers measures the satisfaction of those who chose to travel. ____________________. A company that polls only its current customers will therefore learn little about why others left.
options: It leaves out those who were put off and never boarded, whose views may differ sharply from those of the travellers.
It shows that most people who use trains are satisfied, and it proves that those who stay away must be satisfied as well.
It is the only reliable measure of satisfaction, since those who have not travelled have no views that are worth collecting.
It is useful because it counts the views of every person in the country, whether the person uses trains or does not.
questions.explanation: Answer: the survey leaves out those who were put off and never boarded. Why: the next sentence says a company polling only current customers 'will therefore learn little about why others left', so the blank must point to the missing group. This is selection bias: the sample excludes the people who matter most. Why the others fail: each treats the sample as complete or as proof about non-users.
