CONVERSATION ANALYSIS: Read the following transcript and choose the answer that is closest to each of the questions that are based on the transcript.

Neha Bhatt (Host, Workplace Desk): A year ago, four new labour codes came into effect and replaced twenty-nine older laws. Has life become simpler for employers?

Dr. Suresh Menon (labour economist): On paper, yes. Having four codes instead of twenty-nine means fewer overlapping definitions, fewer registers and fewer inspections that a firm must prepare for. But I would separate the statute from the experience. A statute sets out principles; the rules framed under it, and the way states apply them, decide what a firm actually does on a Monday morning.

Neha Bhatt: So the gains depend on the rules?

Dr. Menon: To a large extent. Labour is a concurrent subject, which means that both the Centre and the states may make rules, and states may differ. A firm that operates in five states may find that a single code has become five slightly different sets of procedure. Consolidation reduces the number of laws, but it does not by itself reduce the number of authorities.

Neha Bhatt: And for workers?

Dr. Menon: The promise is wider coverage, especially for people in informal and platform work, who were outside most of the older laws. But coverage on paper is not protection in practice. It becomes real only when registration is easy, benefits can be carried from one employer to another, and someone checks that the contributions are being made. If those conditions are missing, the worker has a right and no way to use it.

Neha Bhatt: So how should we judge the reform?

Dr. Menon: By outcomes a few years from now, not by the date of notification. I would look at how many people are registered, how long disputes take to settle, and whether small firms report a lighter burden. Those figures will tell us more than the announcement did.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the central argument of the passage?
options: A quarter-point rise in the repo rate is too small to affect households, and the reaction to it was therefore much exaggerated by the press
Central banks should avoid raising rates because the costs fall unequally and the benefits can never be shown to have been produced by the policy
The repo rate matters chiefly because it moves overnight lending, and all other effects of a rate decision are small by comparison with this one
A small rate rise matters because of how it travels through the economy and what people infer, and its success is hard to judge
questions.explanation: Answer: a small rise matters through its route and its signal, and its success is hard to judge. Why: paragraph 1 says importance 'lies in the route by which the decision travels ... and in what people infer from it'; the last paragraph says success is 'peculiarly hard to judge'. Why the others fail: the author says the arithmetic is small but the reaction needs explaining, not that it was exaggerated; paragraph 4 says unequal costs are 'not an argument against a rise'; and the passage stresses the uneven later effects and the expectations channel, not the overnight rate alone. Tip: a main-idea answer must hold the opening problem and the closing difficulty together.

questions.question: According to the passage, a fixed-rate loan differs from a loan linked to the repo rate in that it
options: responds to a change in the policy rate more slowly than a deposit, because banks are quicker to raise what they charge
does not respond to a policy rate change until it is renewed, whereas the linked loan can reprice within a quarter
falls in cost when the policy rate rises, because the bank wishes to attract borrowers whose loans are not linked to it
is repriced by the bank only after it has examined whether its funding costs justify the trouble of making the change
questions.explanation: Answer: a fixed-rate loan does not reprice until renewal, a linked loan can within a quarter. Why: paragraph 2 says a linked loan 'reprices quickly, sometimes within a quarter', while a fixed-rate loan 'does not reprice at all until it is renewed'. Why the others fail: the 'funding costs' phrase in the passage is about DEPOSIT rates, not fixed loans; the passage never says fixed loans become cheaper; and the comparison with deposits is not the one drawn. Tip: check which instrument a quoted phrase actually belongs to.

questions.question: The passage suggests that a rate rise may unsettle an audience instead of calming it when
options: the market suspects the bank knows something worrying that it has not stated, and reads the rise as a sign of alarm
the bank has stated clearly that it expects inflation to be contained and has raised the rate by a small margin
firms and households have already agreed to ask for smaller wage increases and smaller increases in their prices
savers discover that deposit rates have risen by less than the rates that banks charge to the borrowers they lend to
questions.explanation: Answer: when the market reads the rise as alarm because the bank may know something it has not said. Why: paragraph 3 says a rise 'can also be read as a sign of alarm, if the market concludes that the bank knows something worrying that it has not stated'. Why the others fail: a clear statement of expected containment is the calming case; wage and price restraint is the intended outcome, not unsettlement; and the savers' result belongs to the distribution paragraph, not the signalling one. Tip: match the condition in the question to the sentence beginning 'if'.

questions.question: The ship's captain analogy is used to illustrate that
options: central banks cannot control inflation at all, because the forces that move prices are as large as the ocean itself
the public should blame the central bank for the swell, since it is the bank that has set the course of the economy
a central bank must act on a forecast because its actions work slowly, and so may look late or excessive
a rate rise should be postponed until the published inflation figure shows clearly what the bank should do next
questions.explanation: Answer: the bank must act on a forecast because effects are delayed, so a decision may look late or excessive. Why: the paragraph says the published figure 'describes decisions taken some months ago' and that a decision that 'looks late or excessive on the day it is announced may be reasonable in the light of what the forecast showed'. Why the others fail: the author does not say control is impossible; the captain is BLAMED unfairly, which the author does not endorse; and waiting for the published figure is the very error the paragraph warns against. Tip: analogies illustrate one feature; find the feature the paragraph states.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT supported by the passage?
options: Firms that finance themselves from profits are likely to feel the effect of a rate rise less than firms that depend on credit
Households that hold deposits always gain more from a rate rise than households that hold loans lose from it
A government that borrows heavily pays more on each new issue of its bonds when the policy rate rises
The effect of a rate rise on prices may come partly through the expectations that people form about future inflation
questions.explanation: Answer: the claim that depositors always gain more than borrowers lose. Why: paragraph 4 says savers gain 'usually by less than borrowers lose', because banks raise what they charge faster than what they pay. Why the others ARE supported: paragraph 4 (self-financing firms barely notice; heavy borrowers pay more) and paragraph 3 (expectations). Tip: in NOT-questions, words such as 'always' are a red flag and the text usually says the opposite.

questions.question: The author says the success of a rate rise is 'peculiarly hard to judge' because
options: inflation falls in the months after every rate rise, so critics and the bank can never disagree about the result
the bank itself publishes figures only for the months in which its own policy was clearly successful in lowering prices
the monthly instalment on a typical loan changes by so small a sum that households do not notice any difference in cost
the result sought is a non-event that leaves no record, and the fair comparison depends on the quality of a forecast
questions.explanation: Answer: the aim is a non-event that leaves no record, and the fair test needs a forecast. Why: the last paragraph says 'The result that the policy aims at is a thing that does not happen, and a thing that does not happen leaves no record' and that the test is whether the outcome beat 'what the bank itself had forecast without the rise'. Why the others fail: the paragraph says inflation may stay high or fall for other reasons, so disagreement is possible; no selective publication is mentioned; and the instalment point belongs to paragraph 1 and concerns the size of the move, not the judging of success. Tip: use the author's own 'because' clause as the key.

questions.question: The primary purpose of the passage is to
options: argue that the climate conference in Antalya failed because it relied on figures that were exaggerated by the host country
explain why wealthy countries should adopt larger climate targets than poorer countries that have fewer resources to spare
show that counting submitted targets measures participation and not ambition or delivery, while still having a real use
propose that international negotiators should stop collecting national targets and judge countries only by their actual emissions
questions.explanation: Answer: to show that the count measures participation, not ambition or delivery, while explaining why it is still useful. Why: paragraph 1 says 'a count of submissions measures participation, and participation is not the same as ambition'; paragraph 4 begins 'Why, then, keep counting?' and defends the count's function; paragraph 5 calls it 'necessary but insufficient'. Why the others fail: the passage does not call the conference a failure or blame a host; fairness between rich and poor countries is one supporting point, not the aim; and the author does NOT propose abandoning the count. Tip: purpose questions need the whole arc, here a criticism followed by a defence and a balanced close.

questions.question: The comparison with a school that reports how many pupils sat an examination is meant to show that
options: a tally of entries cannot tell a class that passed from one that merely turned up, though it is not worthless
the number of pupils who sit an examination is always a better guide to a school's quality than the marks they obtain
countries that submit their targets late should be treated in the same manner as pupils who arrive late to an examination
a school in which nobody sits the paper deserves no further assessment because it has already failed in its main purpose
questions.explanation: Answer: a tally cannot tell a class that passed from one that turned up, but it is not worthless. Why: paragraph 2 says the figure 'is not worthless, since a school in which nobody sits the paper would be in worse trouble, but it cannot distinguish between a class that has passed and a class that has merely turned up'. Why the others fail: the analogy runs the other way (marks matter more than entries); lateness is not discussed; and the author says the zero-entry school is 'in worse trouble', not that it needs no assessment. Tip: analogies in this passage carry a concession ('not worthless') that wrong options drop.

questions.question: According to the passage, pledges are 'easier to multiply than actions' because
options: the finance negotiations at the conference always end with an agreement that makes action possible for every country concerned
the United Nations Environment Programme has instructed countries to publish targets before they act on them in any manner
pledges can be made only by governments that have already secured the money needed to carry them out
a pledge costs little when made, as the expense falls in later years and on later governments
questions.explanation: Answer: a pledge costs little now because the expense comes later, often for other governments. Why: paragraph 3 says 'A pledge costs little on the day it is made, because the expense falls in later years and often on later governments. This is why pledges are easier to multiply than actions.' Why the others fail: the passage says finance talks took days and a target may rest on 'funds that have not been agreed'; no instruction by the Environment Programme is mentioned; and the last option reverses the point, since a pledge can be made without funds. Tip: 'This is why' points straight back to the cause.

questions.question: Which of the following can be inferred from the paragraph on the differing starting points of countries?
options: Poorer countries should be excused from adopting any target until richer countries have met theirs in full
Two countries with identical targets may make very different efforts, so the tally can hide unequal burdens
A wealthy country's target is always bolder than that of a poorer country because it has more resources available
Negotiators argue about fairness only because they have not understood that the count is a measure of quantity
questions.explanation: Answer: equal targets can hide unequal effort. Why: the paragraph says 'Equal entries in the count therefore conceal unequal burdens' and that a wealthy country may adopt a target that 'looks bold in the tally and costs it little'. Why the others fail: the passage does not recommend excusing poorer countries; it says a rich country's target may LOOK bold but cost little, which refutes 'always bolder'; and negotiators argue about fairness for real reasons, not out of misunderstanding. Tip: inference answers restate the paragraph's logic without adding a policy.

questions.question: The author's description of comparison as 'a form of pressure that costs nothing to apply' suggests that
options: a common format lets governments see what others offer, so one offering less must explain itself at no cost
pressure of this kind is useless, because a form of pressure that costs nothing cannot change what governments do
the common format should be abolished, because it forces governments to reveal information that they would prefer to withhold
countries that offer less than their neighbours will be punished by financial penalties imposed by the conference itself
questions.explanation: Answer: a common format lets governments see what others offer, so one that offers less must explain itself, at no cost. Why: paragraph 4 says 'a government that offers less than its neighbours must explain why. Comparison is a form of pressure that costs nothing to apply.' It adds that transparency 'does not guarantee action, but action is harder to avoid when everyone can watch'. Why the others fail: the author does not call it useless; nothing says the format should be abolished; and no penalties are mentioned (the pressure is explicitly cost-free). Tip: 'costs nothing' praises the method as cheap, not as weak.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the author's claim that a count of national targets is an incomplete measure of progress?
options: Every country that attended the conference in Antalya had submitted its new targets before the conference had begun
The number of countries submitting targets rose between the opening of the conference and the middle of its second week
Several countries that submitted targets on time later emitted more than promised, while some that submitted late cut sharply
Most countries that had submitted targets described them in public statements as ambitious and achievable at modest cost
questions.explanation: Answer: if timely submitters later emitted more than promised while late submitters cut sharply, the count (who submitted) and the outcome (what happened) separate. Why: the passage argues that participation is not ambition and pledges are not actions; this evidence directly shows both gaps. Why the others do not strengthen: universal submission and a rising count are exactly what the count shows without testing outcomes; and public statements of ambition are self-description, not evidence of delivery. Tip: to strengthen 'X measures Y poorly', find evidence in which X and Y diverge.

questions.question: Which of the following best states the main point of the passage?
options: Consent managers should replace the regulator, since an intermediary can protect individuals better than any public authority
Consent is weak unless refusal is genuinely possible, and limits on what firms may collect protect people more reliably
The data protection law is flawed because it permits firms to collect information without informing the individuals concerned
Individuals should read every notice carefully, since the entire protection offered by the law depends on informed consent
questions.explanation: Answer: consent is weak unless refusal is possible, and limits on collection protect more reliably. Why: the opening says a consent given without understanding 'is a poor safeguard'; paragraph 5 says 'Consent means something only if the person can refuse and still obtain the service'; paragraph 5 on purpose limitation calls it 'the sturdier of the two protections'. Why the others fail: the manager is registered with the regulator and may itself pose risks; the law is not said to allow collection without notice; and the passage says almost nobody can reasonably read every notice. Tip: look for the claim that links the earlier paragraphs, here 'consent depends on conditions'.

questions.question: According to the passage, 'consent fatigue' arises because
options: the effort of reading every notice exceeds the benefit of reading any one, so almost nobody reads them
firms are legally forbidden from using the data they collect for any purpose other than the stated one
the intermediary registered with the regulator is unable to cancel permissions that were given long ago
individuals are unwilling to share any information about themselves with firms that offer them a service
questions.explanation: Answer: reading every notice costs more than any one is worth, so nobody reads. Why: paragraph 2 says 'The effort of reading all of them exceeds any benefit that one person can expect from reading any one, and so almost nobody does' and then 'Economists call the result consent fatigue'. Why the others fail: purpose limitation is a separate safeguard in a later paragraph; the consent manager is described as able to cancel old permissions; and the passage says people tick the box, so they are not unwilling to share. Tip: the sentence containing the term, or just before it, gives the definition.

questions.question: The author raises the risk that an intermediary may be 'paid by the firms that want the data' to point out that
options: firms are legally forbidden from paying any fee to an intermediary that is registered with the regulator
an intermediary will always favour the firms because it cannot operate without payment from some source
individuals cannot use an intermediary unless they agree to pay a fee for each permission they manage
its loyalty to the individual may weaken, so the design needs rules that align its incentives with his
questions.explanation: Answer: its loyalty may be weakened, so rules must align its incentives. Why: paragraph 3 says that if the intermediary is paid by firms 'its loyalty to the individual may be quietly weakened' and that 'The design therefore depends on rules that keep the intermediary's incentives aligned'. Why the others fail: no legal ban on fees is mentioned; 'always favour' overstates a risk the author calls only possible; and fees charged to individuals are not discussed. Tip: 'may' in the text should not become 'will always' in the answer.

questions.question: Which of the following is a feature of a 'dark pattern' as described in the passage?
options: It requires the person to read and sign a long notice before any information about them may be used by the firm
It allows a person to withdraw consent at any time by a single tap in the application that obtained it from them
It makes agreeing quick and easy by a single tap, while making refusal depend on a long search through several different screens
It prevents a firm from collecting any information other than what is needed for the purpose that it has stated
questions.explanation: Answer: it makes agreeing easy and refusing laborious. Why: the added paragraph says 'agreeing takes a single tap while declining requires a search through several screens' and calls this 'a dark pattern'. Why the others fail: a long signed notice is the opposite of a one-tap design; easy withdrawal is the safeguard the author recommends; and limiting collection is purpose limitation. Tip: match the definition's key contrast: easy to agree, hard to decline.

questions.question: The passage implies that purpose limitation is a 'sturdier' protection than consent because it
options: asks each individual to review the practices of every firm and then to decide whether to grant a permission
depends on conditions such as the ease of refusal, which are present in most services that people use
replaces the regulator with a system in which firms are checked only by the intermediaries that serve individuals
places the burden on the firm, which can inspect its practices, and works even if no one reads the notice
questions.explanation: Answer: the burden is on the firm, and it works even if nobody reads the notice. Why: the paragraph says purpose limitation 'shifts the burden from the person, who cannot be expected to inspect every practice, to the firm, which can' and 'works even when nobody reads the notice'. Why the others fail: individual review is the weakness of consent; the 'conditions' phrase describes consent, which 'depends on conditions that may not exist'; and nothing says intermediaries replace the regulator. Tip: sturdier means it relies on fewer fragile assumptions.

questions.question: Which of the following would the author most likely regard as the best test of whether a data protection law truly protects people?
options: The cost to an individual of refusing a data request, in terms of the service that he would lose
How many consents have been recorded by the intermediaries that are registered with the regulator in the year
How long the notices that firms present to users are, and how carefully they have been drafted by lawyers
How many firms have applied to the regulator for the registration needed to operate as a consent manager
questions.explanation: Answer: the cost to the individual of saying no. Why: the final sentence says a law should examine 'less the number of consents obtained, and more the real cost to the individual of saying no'. Why the others fail: the number of recorded consents is exactly what the author says to examine LESS; notice length and quality of drafting do not address real choice; and the number of applicants measures activity, not protection. Tip: the closing sentence often holds the author's own test.

questions.question: Dr. Menon's distinction between 'the statute' and 'the experience' implies that
options: the statute is irrelevant to firms, since the experience of compliance is decided entirely by the officials who inspect them
the new codes have made no difference to firms, because the older laws were enforced in the same manner as the new codes
rules framed under a law and their state application decide what a firm does, so the text alone misleads
states should be prevented from framing their own rules so that the statute may govern the firm's daily conduct
questions.explanation: Answer: rules and state application decide what a firm does, so the text alone is a poor guide. Why: he says 'A statute sets out principles; the rules framed under it, and the way states apply them, decide what a firm actually does on a Monday morning.' Why the others fail: he does not call the statute irrelevant; he grants that on paper the position is simpler; and he does not recommend limiting states, only notes that they may differ. Tip: contrast words ('separate X from Y') mark where the speaker places the weight.

questions.question: Dr. Menon says that 'consolidation reduces the number of laws, but it does not by itself reduce the number of authorities'. This is because
options: each of the four codes is administered by a separate ministry, so the firm must deal with four offices instead of twenty-nine
labour is a concurrent subject, so Centre and states both make rules, and a multi-state firm may meet several procedures
the older laws were enforced by a single national authority, which the new codes have replaced with many state authorities
firms operating in several states are exempt from the codes and must follow the procedures of their home state alone
questions.explanation: Answer: labour is a concurrent subject, so both Centre and states make rules, and multi-state firms may face several procedures. Why: he says 'Labour is a concurrent subject, which means that both the Centre and the states may make rules ... A firm that operates in five states may find that a single code has become five slightly different sets of procedure.' Why the others fail: separate ministries are not mentioned; a single national authority for the old laws is not claimed; and no exemption for multi-state firms is stated. Tip: the 'because' in the question is answered in the line immediately before the statement.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes Dr. Menon's view of how the reform should be judged?
options: By outcomes some years later, such as registrations, dispute times and small-firm burden, not by the date of notification
By the number of old laws that have been repealed, since a smaller body of law is itself evidence of success
By the satisfaction of large firms, which are best placed to describe how the codes affect their daily operations
By the speed with which all states have notified their rules, since delay is the only real obstacle to the reform
questions.explanation: Answer: by outcomes a few years later, not by the date of notification. Why: his closing line says 'By outcomes a few years from now, not by the date of notification' and lists registrations, dispute duration and small-firm burden. Why the others fail: he says consolidation reduces laws but not authorities, so the count of repealed laws is not the test; large firms are not singled out, and he mentions small firms; and rule notification is a means, while he names several obstacles including enforcement and portability. Tip: when a speaker says 'not by X', X is never the answer.

questions.question: The company's early success proved ________, for the fashion that had made its product popular faded within a season and left it with unsold stock.
options: enduring
venerable
ephemeral
robust
questions.explanation: Answer: 'ephemeral' means lasting a very short time. The clue is 'faded within a season'. The others: 'enduring' (lasting) and 'robust' (strong, durable) are opposites of what the sentence describes; 'venerable' (worthy of respect because of age) does not suit something that vanished quickly. Tip: the clause after 'for' explains the blank.

questions.question: The minister's reply was so ________ that reporters, after reading it twice, could still not say whether the proposal had been accepted or abandoned.
options: incisive
nebulous
emphatic
forthright
questions.explanation: Answer: 'nebulous' means vague and unclear in form. The clue is that the reporters 'could still not say' what the reply meant. The others: 'incisive' (sharp and clear), 'emphatic' (forceful and unmistakable) and 'forthright' (direct and frank) would all have made the meaning plain. Tip: when the outcome is confusion, the blank is a word for vagueness.

questions.question: Having been repeatedly praised by those who stood to benefit from his favour, the director grew ________, and mistook flattery for honest assessment.
options: vigilant
diffident
scrupulous
complacent
questions.explanation: Answer: 'complacent' means smugly satisfied and unaware of any need for improvement. The clue is that he 'mistook flattery for honest assessment'. The others: 'vigilant' (watchful), 'diffident' (shy, lacking confidence) and 'scrupulous' (careful about what is right) do not follow from being praised or explain such a mistake. Tip: ask what attitude praise breeds when it is undeserved.

questions.question: The report's findings were deliberately ________: it described the policy as 'broadly successful' while quietly ________ the figures that showed it had missed its main targets, so that readers were ________ without a single false statement.
options: guarded; highlighting; misled
guarded; omitting; misled
candid; omitting; misled
guarded; omitting; informed
questions.explanation: Answer: guarded; omitting; misled. Step by step. A report that says 'broadly successful' and hides unfavourable figures is 'guarded' (cautious in what it reveals); it 'omits' the figures that show missed targets; and readers are 'misled' without any false statement. 'Highlighting' the figures would contradict 'quietly'; 'candid' (frank) contradicts the hiding; 'informed' contradicts the point that readers were deceived by omission. Tip: 'without a single false statement' tells you the deception is by omission.

questions.question: A leader who is ________ to criticism will seldom learn from error; the wiser course is to ________ dissent, since a colleague who disagrees may ________ a flaw that the leader has missed.
options: impervious; welcome; expose
receptive; welcome; expose
impervious; suppress; expose
impervious; welcome; conceal
questions.explanation: Answer: impervious; welcome; expose. Step by step. 'Seldom learn from error' needs someone closed to criticism: 'impervious' (not affected by it). 'The wiser course' is the opposite, to 'welcome' dissent, because a dissenting colleague may 'expose' (reveal) a flaw. 'Receptive' would make the first clause illogical; 'suppress' is the unwise course, not the wiser one; 'conceal' reverses the benefit of dissent. Tip: 'wiser course' signals an advice that opposes the first clause.

questions.question: The treaty was a ________ achievement: it ended a war that had lasted a generation, yet its terms were so ________ that each side soon found grounds to ________ it.
options: momentous; precise; contest
trivial; ambiguous; contest
momentous; ambiguous; honour
momentous; ambiguous; contest
questions.explanation: Answer: momentous; ambiguous; contest. Step by step. Ending a generation-long war is 'momentous' (of great importance). 'Yet' signals a turn: its terms were 'ambiguous' (open to two readings), so each side found grounds to 'contest' (dispute) it. 'Precise' terms would leave no grounds for dispute; 'trivial' contradicts ending a long war; 'honour' contradicts 'yet' and the grounds each side found. Tip: 'yet' introduces a contrast with the praise before it.

questions.question: The scheme, which was widely ________ as a model of efficiency, proved ________ on inspection: its savings were ________ by costs that had simply been moved to another department's account.
options: hailed; genuine; offset
dismissed; illusory; offset
hailed; illusory; offset
hailed; illusory; confirmed
questions.explanation: Answer: hailed; illusory; offset. Step by step. A scheme widely 'hailed' (praised) as efficient, which on inspection proved 'illusory' (not real), because its savings were 'offset' (cancelled) by costs moved elsewhere. 'Genuine' contradicts the moved costs; 'dismissed' does not fit 'widely ... as a model of efficiency'; 'confirmed' would mean the costs supported the savings, the opposite of the point. Tip: the 'on inspection' contrast tells you the first word is positive and the second negative.

questions.question: Because the data were ________, the analyst refused to draw a firm conclusion; she preferred to ________ judgement until further evidence arrived rather than ________ a theory on figures that might later be revised.
options: inconclusive; hasten; stake
decisive; suspend; stake
inconclusive; suspend; stake
inconclusive; suspend; abandon
questions.explanation: Answer: inconclusive; suspend; stake. Step by step. Refusing a firm conclusion means the data did not settle the matter: 'inconclusive'. She would 'suspend' (put off) judgement and not 'stake' (risk, rest) a theory on figures that might be revised. 'Decisive' data would not justify refusing; 'hasten' judgement contradicts 'until further evidence'; 'abandon' a theory does not fit 'rather than ... a theory on figures that might later be revised', which needs a word for committing. Tip: 'rather than' marks the unwanted action.

questions.question: The ________ vehicle blocked the road while the clerk, who had gone to buy ________ for the office, argued about the ________ of the parking order.
options: stationery; stationary; validity
stationary; stationary; validity
stationary; stationery; validation
stationary; stationery; validity
questions.explanation: Answer: stationary; stationery; validity. STATIONARY (adjective) means not moving (a stationary vehicle); STATIONERY (noun) means paper, pens and office supplies (the 'e' in 'paper' and 'envelope' helps you remember it). VALIDITY means the state of being legally or logically sound (the validity of an order); VALIDATION means the act of confirming. Swapping the first two words reads 'stationery vehicle' and 'stationary for the office'. Tip: 'stationEry' goes with 'envElopes'.

questions.question: The speaker's steady ________ of the platform drew the crowd's ________, and after a final ________ from the chair, the motion was carried.
options: ascent; assent; assent
ascent; assent; ascent
assent; ascent; assent
ascent; ascent; assent
questions.explanation: Answer: ascent; assent; assent. ASCENT is the act of climbing, so the speaker's steady 'ascent' of the platform; ASSENT is agreement, so the crowd's 'assent' and the chair's final 'assent'. The other combinations put 'assent' where a climb is meant, or 'ascent' where agreement is meant. Tip: ASCENT has 'sc' as in 'scale' (to climb); ASSENT has 'ss' like a double yes.

questions.question: The minister's aides tried to ________ the report before publication, but the court ruled that officials may not ________ news of public interest, and a formal ________ of the aides was recorded.
options: censure; suppress; censor
censor; suppress; censure
censor; suppress; censor
censor; surpass; censure
questions.explanation: Answer: censor; suppress; censure. CENSOR (verb) means to cut or ban material; CENSURE means formal criticism or disapproval; SUPPRESS means to hold back or put down; SURPASS means to exceed. The aides tried to 'censor' the report; officials may not 'suppress' news; and a formal 'censure' of the aides was recorded. The other options swap censor and censure or use 'surpass'. Tip: a censor cuts; a censure scolds.

questions.question: One of the statements below contains a word used incorrectly or inappropriately. Choose the option which has the incorrect or inappropriate usage of the word.
options: The crisis taught the bank a costly lesson about lending without security.
Better hedging can lessen a firm's exposure to sudden currency swings.
The professor's lesson on inflation was attended by every student in the batch.
The new rule is intended to lesson the burden on small firms.
questions.explanation: Answer: the sentence 'to lesson the burden'. LESSEN (verb) means to reduce; LESSON (noun) is something taught or learnt. The rule is meant to 'lessen' the burden. The other sentences are correct: 'a costly lesson' (noun), 'lessen a firm's exposure' (verb) and 'The professor's lesson' (noun). Tip: after 'to', you need a verb, so the verb 'lessen'.

questions.question: The policy aims to reduce costs, improve access, and <u>increasing</u> transparency across all branches.
options: increased
to be increasing
increase
an increase in
questions.explanation: Answer: 'increase'. Rule: parallel structure. After 'aims to', the three items must share one form: reduce, improve and increase. 'Increasing' is a different form and breaks the list; 'increased' is a past form; 'to be increasing' and 'an increase in' change the grammar of the item. Tip: items in a list must share one grammatical form.

questions.question: The committee received <u>less</u> complaints this year than in any previous year since its founding.
options: fewer
lesser
little
least
questions.explanation: Answer: 'fewer'. Rule: use 'fewer' with countable plural nouns (complaints) and 'less' with uncountable nouns (less money, less time). 'Lesser' means smaller in importance; 'little' is used with uncountable nouns; 'least' is a superlative and does not fit the comparison with 'than'. Tip: if you can count them, use 'fewer'.

questions.question: By the time the new rule is notified, most firms <u>will already adapt</u> their systems to the draft.
options: have already adapted
will already have adapted
already adapted
would already adapt
questions.explanation: Answer: 'will already have adapted'. Rule: the future perfect (will have + past participle) describes an action completed before a stated future time ('by the time the new rule is notified'). 'Have already adapted' is a present perfect and does not fit the future reference; 'already adapted' is a simple past; 'would already adapt' is a conditional and does not express completion. Tip: 'by the time' with a future event usually asks for the future perfect.

questions.question: The regulator insisted that the firm <u>discloses</u> the data to the public before the end of the month.
options: disclosed
will disclose
disclose
is disclosing
questions.explanation: Answer: 'disclose'. Rule: after verbs of demand, request or insistence (insist, demand, recommend, require) that introduce a 'that' clause, English uses the subjunctive: the bare verb form regardless of the subject ('that the firm disclose'). 'Disclosed', 'will disclose' and 'is disclosing' are the indicative forms and do not express a demand. Tip: insist/demand/require + that + subject + base verb.

questions.question:
Complete the paragraph logically:

A count of the countries that have submitted climate targets tells us how many have taken part. ____________________. A school that reports only the number of pupils who sat the examination has told us something, but not what we most wish to know.
options: It does not tell us how ambitious the targets are, nor whether the governments that made them will carry them out in time.
It tells us exactly how much the world's emissions will fall, since every target that has been submitted will be met.
It shows that governments are indifferent to the problem, because no government would make a target if it cared.
It is of no use at all, because a country that submits a target has already done everything that is required.
questions.explanation: Answer: the count does not tell us the ambition or the delivery. Why: the following sentence compares the count to a school reporting only the number who sat the examination, 'something, but not what we most wish to know', which needs a blank saying what the count leaves out. Why the others fail: the count cannot tell exactly how emissions will fall; the cynical claim is unsupported; and 'of no use at all' contradicts 'has told us something'. Tip: the analogy afterwards must fit the blank in both directions.

questions.question:
Complete the paragraph logically:

If inflation falls after a rate rise, the central bank may claim the credit. ____________________. The fair test is therefore to compare the outcome with what would have happened without the rise, and that can only be estimated.
options: Inflation always falls after a rate rise, so the central bank is right to claim the credit in every case.
But prices may have fallen for other reasons, such as a good harvest, so the fall alone proves little.
The central bank should therefore avoid publishing any forecast, so that no one can compare its outcomes with it.
A fall in inflation is evidence that the rise was unnecessary, since prices would have fallen of their own accord.
questions.explanation: Answer: prices may have fallen for other reasons, so the fall alone does not show the policy worked. Why: the next sentence calls for comparison with 'what would have happened without the rise', which follows from doubting that the fall proves success. Why the others fail: 'always falls' contradicts the passage's logic and makes the next sentence pointless; publishing no forecast contradicts the need for comparison; and 'unnecessary' goes too far, since the fall might equally be due to the rise. Tip: 'therefore' in the following sentence draws on a doubt raised in the blank.

questions.question:
Complete the paragraph logically:

A person who is asked to consent faces hundreds of long notices. ____________________. This is why, in practice, a consent is often a formality and not a decision.
options: Each notice is short, clear and easy to understand, and so most people read it carefully before they agree to it.
The firms that write the notices are legally required to explain every term to each person in a face-to-face meeting.
People who refuse to tick the box are always given the service on the same terms as those who agree to the notice.
The effort needed to read them all exceeds the benefit of reading any one, so most people tick without reading.
questions.explanation: Answer: the effort to read them exceeds the benefit, so most tick without reading. Why: the closing sentence says consent is 'often a formality and not a decision', which follows if people do not read. Why the others fail: short and clear notices would make reading likely, contradicting the conclusion; face-to-face explanation is an unsupported invention; and equal terms for refusers would make consent a real choice, the opposite of a formality. Tip: the final sentence usually states what the blank must lead to.

questions.question:
Rearrange the five sentences (1-5) into a logical sequence (Type the 5-digit sequence as answer):

1. Savers gain, but usually by less than borrowers lose.
2. A rise in the policy rate does not fall evenly on everyone.
3. Firms that depend on credit feel it first, while those that finance themselves from profits barely notice it.
4. The decision in the policy statement therefore hides a long list of winners and losers.
5. Banks are quicker to raise what they charge than what they pay.
questions.explanation: Answer: 2-1-5-3-4. Step by step. Sentence 2 opens with the general claim (it does not fall evenly). Sentence 1 gives the first case (savers gain, but by less). Sentence 5 explains why ('Banks are quicker...'). Sentence 3 turns to a second case (firms that depend on credit). Sentence 4 begins 'therefore' and concludes. Tip: an explanation ('why') usually follows the statement it explains, and 'therefore' closes.

questions.question:
Rearrange the five sentences (1-5) into a logical sequence (Type the 5-digit sequence as answer):

1. A target is a public commitment that others can read.
2. Such a count measures participation, and not ambition.
3. More countries had submitted new targets by November than by the start of the month.
4. Yet the figure cannot show whether the promises are large, or whether they will be kept.
5. The count is therefore a necessary measure, but an insufficient one.
questions.explanation: Answer: 3-1-2-4-5. Step by step. Sentence 3 opens with the fact (more countries have submitted). Sentence 1 says what a target is and why the count matters. Sentence 2 begins 'Such a count' and gives the limit (participation, not ambition). Sentence 4 begins 'Yet the figure' and adds the further limits. Sentence 5 begins 'therefore' and concludes. Tip: 'Such a ...' and 'the figure' refer back to the count introduced earlier.

questions.question:
Rearrange the four sentences (1-4) into a logical sequence (Type the 4-digit sequence as answer):

1. Even then, a person who cannot refuse without losing the service has no real choice.
2. A person is asked to consent through a long notice that almost nobody reads.
3. An intermediary that lets people manage permissions in one place may help.
4. The remedy, however, must address the design of the choice and not merely its record.
questions.explanation: Answer: 2-3-1-4. Step by step. Sentence 2 states the problem (consent through unread notices). Sentence 3 proposes an improvement (an intermediary). Sentence 1 begins 'Even then' and says the improvement is not enough if refusal costs the service. Sentence 4 begins 'The remedy, however' and states the real requirement. Tip: 'Even then' follows a remedy and points to its limit.

questions.question:
Rearrange the five sentences (1-5) into a logical sequence (Type the 5-digit sequence as answer):

1. A labour statute sets out principles, but the rules under it decide what a firm does.
2. Four codes now stand where twenty-nine laws once did.
3. Because states may frame their own rules, a firm in five states may meet five procedures.
4. The reform should therefore be judged by outcomes some years from now.
5. On paper, the consolidation makes life simpler for employers.
questions.explanation: Answer: 2-5-1-3-4. Step by step. Sentence 2 states the fact (four codes replaced twenty-nine laws). Sentence 5 draws the paper conclusion (simpler). Sentence 1 qualifies with the contrast between statute and rules. Sentence 3 begins 'Because states may frame their own rules' and gives the example of the difficulty. Sentence 4 begins 'therefore' and concludes how to judge. Tip: 'On paper' invites a later 'but' idea, which sentence 1 supplies.

questions.question:
Rearrange the four sentences (1-4) into a logical sequence (Type the 4-digit sequence as answer):

1. A central bank must therefore act on a forecast, and not on the figure published today.
2. That figure describes the effects of decisions taken some months earlier.
3. The effects of a rate rise arrive late.
4. A decision that looks excessive today may be reasonable in the light of the forecast.
questions.explanation: Answer: 3-1-2-4. Step by step. Sentence 3 opens with the general fact (effects arrive late). Sentence 1 begins 'therefore' and draws the consequence (act on a forecast, not today's figure). Sentence 2 begins 'That figure', which refers to 'the figure published today' in sentence 1, so it must follow it. Sentence 4 closes with the result for how a decision may look. Tip: 'That figure' needs the figure to have been mentioned just before.

title: IPMAT Indore VA Sectional – 26th Nov 2026 (Advanced Analytical – High Difficulty)

passages.RC1:
Official figures for India's growth in the July-September quarter are due on 30 November, and the guessing has already produced a spread. The finance ministry's model puts growth at 7.35 per cent, the central bank had projected 7.2, and a research team at a large bank has estimated about 7.8, using a statistical model built on 54 high-frequency indicators. A gap of half a percentage point may look small, but in an economy of this size it represents a large sum of money. More interesting than the gap is what it reveals: the figure that will be announced is not simply read from a counter. It is assembled, and it is assembled late.

The delay arises because an economy cannot be measured while it is moving. To compute output for a quarter, statisticians need returns from firms, surveys of households and records of farm production, and these arrive weeks or months after the period has ended. Some are incomplete, and the missing parts are filled by estimates that are later revised. The first release of a figure is thus a provisional judgement, and it is not unusual for the revised number to differ from it by an amount that exceeds the gap between rival forecasters. Anyone who treats the first announcement as the settled truth has misunderstood what it is.

Forecasters have therefore turned to what is called nowcasting. Instead of waiting for the slow and complete data, they use fast and imperfect indicators that are available almost at once: electricity use, port traffic, tax collections, vehicle sales and credit growth. Each indicator is a poor guide taken singly, since electricity use can rise because of a hot summer and not because of a factory boom. But a model that combines dozens of them can find the pattern that they share, and when it works, it produces a figure weeks before the official one. The finance ministry has begun to publish such an estimate, and banks have built their own.

Why, then, do the models disagree? The reason is that each rests on choices. One must decide which indicators to include, how much weight each deserves, and how closely the past relationship between the indicators and output will hold in the present. A model trained on years in which formal firms dominated may misjudge a quarter in which informal activity behaved differently. Two skilled teams, looking at the same data and making reasonable choices, can arrive at different answers, and the disagreement is a fair measure of how much the data can tell us at this stage.

A further source of confusion lies in the name of the figure itself. The headline number is gross domestic product, but analysts also quote gross value added, and the two can differ noticeably: the bank that estimates GDP growth at about 7.8 per cent expects value added to grow by between 8 and 8.2 per cent. The difference arises because GDP adds taxes on products and subtracts subsidies to the value that producers add. A quarter in which subsidies rise, or in which tax collections lag, can therefore widen the gap, and a reader who compares a forecast of one figure with the release of the other will believe that someone has erred when no one has.

The sensible reader of such forecasts will avoid two errors. The first is to treat the average of the forecasts as the truth, as though the errors of different models were certain to cancel; they may instead share a common blind spot, such as a sector that none of the indicators captures. The second is to treat the spread as a sign that forecasting is worthless. The spread, rather, is information: it tells us how uncertain the quarter is, and a wide spread should make the headline figure, when it comes, a subject of questions as much as of celebration.
passages.RC2:
When this year's prize in economic sciences went to Robert Hall and Michael Woodford for their work on the microeconomic foundations of stabilising the economy, a member of the prize committee summed up the history in a few words: the Keynesian recipe worked well until it didn't. The recipe, as developed after the Great Depression, was simple. When demand falls and unemployment rises, the government should spend or cut taxes to raise demand; when demand surges and prices rise, it should do the reverse. For three decades the formula appeared to serve. Then came the 1970s, when prices and unemployment rose together, and the recipe seemed to have nothing to say.

The old method had relied on relationships measured in aggregate data: between spending and income, or between unemployment and inflation. It assumed that these relationships were stable, and that a policymaker could therefore use them as levers. The difficulty is that the relationships are not laws of nature. They are the outcome of millions of decisions by households and firms, and those decisions depend on what the people making them expect. When policy changes, expectations change, and the relationships that were measured under the old policy may shift beneath the policymaker's hand. A lever that moved the economy last year may do something else this year because people have learnt how it works.

The laureates' contribution was to rebuild the theory from the bottom. Instead of postulating a relationship between aggregates, they modelled how a household decides whether to save or spend and how a firm decides whether to change its prices, and then derived the aggregate behaviour from these decisions. Such an approach has a decisive advantage: it can predict how behaviour will respond to a new policy, since the model contains the reasons for the behaviour and not merely its past record. A model that knows why people act is better placed to say what they will do when circumstances change.

One result of this approach is the importance of what a central bank says. If households and firms form expectations about future interest rates, then a statement about the likely path of those rates can influence spending today, without any change in the rate itself. Woodford has argued that stabilisation cannot be treated as a matter of pulling levers independently of what people understand. In the years following the financial crisis of the late 2000s, when rates could not be cut much further, explicit statements about the future path of policy became a significant part of the response.

An example shows why this matters. Suppose a government believes that it can lower unemployment permanently by tolerating a little more inflation, because the data of the past show that the two have moved in opposite directions. If it acts on that belief, workers and firms will soon come to expect the higher inflation and will build it into their wage demands and prices. The old relationship then disappears, and the economy is left with the higher inflation and no lasting gain in jobs. The pattern in the data was real, but it depended on people not anticipating the policy that was designed to exploit it.

None of this means that the bottom-up approach is free of difficulty. A model built on decisions must make assumptions about how people reason, and if those assumptions are unrealistic, the elegance of the structure will not save it. The lesson of the prize is therefore a modest one. A theory that rests on the reasons for behaviour will usually travel better than one that rests on past correlations, but it travels well only if the reasons it assumes are close to the reasons that people really have.
passages.RC3:
India's electric vehicle market offers a lesson in how to read growth. In October, total electric vehicle registrations reached 354,378, a rise of more than 51 per cent over the same month a year earlier. Electric cars alone have sold more than 30,000 units a month for five consecutive months, and the total for the first ten months of the year has reached 293,877. Yet in the same month, the share of electric vehicles in all vehicle sales fell, to about 11 per cent. Both statements are true. They are not in conflict, but they answer different questions, and a reader who confuses them will draw the wrong conclusion.

The first statistic measures volume: how many electric vehicles were sold. The second measures penetration: what fraction of all sales they formed. Volume can rise while penetration falls if the total market grows faster than the electric segment. This is what the figure for October signals, namely that overall vehicle sales expanded more quickly than electric sales did. The same arithmetic applies in any growing market. A shop whose sales of a product double is losing ground relative to its rivals if the whole market has tripled.

The choice between the two measures depends on what one wishes to know. For a manufacturer planning a factory or a government planning charging stations, volume is the relevant figure, since it determines the demand to be served. For a policy-maker concerned with emissions or oil imports, penetration matters more, because the change in fuel use depends on what share of the fleet is electric and not on how many electric vehicles are sold in a given month. A policy that is judged by volume may look successful even as it fails to alter the composition of the market.

A related trap is the base effect. Growth is calculated against an earlier figure, and when that figure is small, a modest increase in absolute terms produces a large percentage. A month in which electric car sales rise from about 13,000 units to about 21,000 a year later shows growth of more than sixty per cent, and a market that adds the same number of units to a larger base will show far less. High growth rates in the early stage of a technology are therefore less impressive than they appear, and the slowing of growth later is not necessarily a sign of failure; it may be the arithmetic of a larger base.

The timing of growth deserves a similar caution. New technologies tend to follow an S-shaped path: adoption is slow while the product is costly and unfamiliar, then quickens as prices fall and charging points multiply, and finally levels off as the market approaches saturation. A reader who looks only at the steep middle of the curve may conclude that rapid growth will continue indefinitely, and a reader who looks only at the early flat stretch may dismiss the technology as a failure. Where on the curve a market currently stands matters at least as much as the rate at which it is moving.

Last year offered a reminder that adoption also responds to its rivals. When indirect tax cuts made petrol and diesel vehicles cheaper, the momentum of electric two-wheelers cooled, even as electric cars and three-wheelers continued to grow. A technology's progress, in other words, depends on the relative price of what it competes with, as well as on its own merits. The disciplined analyst therefore asks three questions of any growth story: growth of what, measured against what, and relative to which alternative?
passages.CA1:
CONVERSATION ANALYSIS: Read the following transcript and choose the answer that is closest to each of the questions that are based on the transcript.

Aarti Rao (Host, Careers Desk): A company has built a tool that screens résumés and recommends whom to interview. It was trained on ten years of the company's own hiring decisions, and the vendor says it matches the recruiters' choices ninety per cent of the time. That sounds impressive, doesn't it?

Dr. Kabir Anand (data scientist): It sounds impressive until you ask what the tool is being matched to. If it agrees with the recruiters ninety per cent of the time, then it has learnt to do what the recruiters did. That is a measure of imitation, not of quality. Whether those recruiters picked good employees is a separate question that the figure does not answer.

Aarti Rao: But surely past decisions are the only data we have.

Dr. Anand: They are the data we have, which is not the same as the data we need. Suppose that, for years, the firm rarely interviewed graduates of smaller colleges. The tool will learn that such graduates are rarely hired, and will rank them low, and we shall never learn whether they would have done well, because they were never given the chance. The pattern is reinforced by its own output.

Aarti Rao: So the tool is biased?

Dr. Anand: I would put it differently. The tool is faithful, and what it is faithful to may be flawed. The remedy is not to abandon such tools, but to test them against outcomes, such as how the people hired actually performed, and to allow a small number of candidates through who would have been screened out, so that the firm can find out whether it was right to screen them.

Aarti Rao: That costs the firm something.

Dr. Anand: It does, and it is the price of knowing.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the central idea of the passage?
options: Forecasters who use many indicators are always more accurate than the statisticians who prepare the official figure after the quarter has ended
The disagreement between forecasting teams shows that growth cannot be measured, so that official figures should not be published or discussed
A single bank's estimate of growth should be preferred over the others because its model uses a larger number of high-frequency indicators
An official growth figure is an assembled, provisional estimate, and the spread among forecasts is itself evidence of uncertainty
questions.explanation: Answer: the official figure is assembled and provisional, and the spread of forecasts shows the uncertainty. Why: paragraph 1 says the figure 'is assembled, and it is assembled late'; paragraph 2 calls the first release 'a provisional judgement'; the last paragraph says 'The spread, rather, is information'. Why the others fail: the author never says forecasters are always more accurate (they may share blind spots); the author rejects the view that the spread makes forecasting 'worthless'; and no model is recommended over others. Tip: a main-idea answer should keep both the 'provisional' point and the 'spread is information' point.

questions.question: According to the passage, the first announcement of a growth figure should not be treated as settled because
options: it is prepared by statisticians who have no access to the surveys of households or the records of farm production
it rests on late, incomplete returns whose gaps are estimated and later revised, sometimes by more than forecasters differ
it is always revised downward after a few weeks, when the missing returns from the informal sector have arrived
it is calculated from the same high-frequency indicators that the forecasting models use, and so shares their errors
questions.explanation: Answer: it relies on late, incomplete returns, filled by estimates later revised, and the revision may exceed the forecasters' gap. Why: paragraph 2 says returns 'arrive weeks or months after the period has ended', 'the missing parts are filled by estimates that are later revised', and the revision may 'exceed the gap between rival forecasters'. Why the others fail: statisticians DO use surveys and farm records; the passage never says revision is always downward; and the official figure uses slow, complete data, in contrast to the fast indicators of nowcasting. Tip: 'always' and 'downward' are unsupported specifics.

questions.question: The author says that electricity use is 'a poor guide taken singly' in order to show that
options: one indicator can move for reasons unrelated to output, so a model combines many to find their shared pattern
electricity use should be removed from nowcasting models because it is always unrelated to the growth of the economy
nowcasting is unreliable because every indicator that it uses can be affected by the weather in the quarter
factories that use a great deal of electricity are less important to the economy than those in the services sector
questions.explanation: Answer: a single indicator can move for unrelated reasons, so models combine many to find the shared pattern. Why: paragraph 3 says electricity use 'can rise because of a hot summer and not because of a factory boom. But a model that combines dozens of them can find the pattern that they share'. Why the others fail: the author does not say electricity is always unrelated; 'every indicator' affected by weather overstates a single example; the sector comparison is not made. Tip: a 'But' sentence after an example states the author's conclusion.

questions.question: Which of the following explains why two skilled teams might arrive at different forecasts from the same data?
options: One team must be using data that is incorrect, since competent forecasters examining the same figures would reach the same result
Some of the teams are required to publish their forecasts before the others and so cannot revise them after the data arrive
They may choose different indicators and weights, and differ on how far past relationships will hold now
The teams measure different things, such as the growth of the informal sector and the growth of the formal sector
questions.explanation: Answer: different choices of indicators, weights and assumptions about the stability of past relationships. Why: paragraph 4 says 'each rests on choices: which indicators to include, how much weight each deserves, and how closely the past relationship ... will hold'. Why the others fail: the author says 'reasonable choices' can still lead to different answers, so incorrect data is not required; the order of publication is not mentioned; and the passage treats the models as forecasting the same quantity. Tip: look for the sentence that begins with 'The reason is that'.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT mentioned or implied as a way in which a reader might be misled by forecasts or releases?
options: Treating the average of several forecasts as the truth, although the models may share a common blind spot in some sector
Regarding the finance ministry's forecast as less reliable than a bank's, since the ministry has a stake in the result
Comparing a forecast of one measure of output with the release of a different measure of output, as though they were the same
Taking the first announcement as the final word, although later revisions may be larger than the gaps among forecasters
questions.explanation: Answer: the idea that the ministry's forecast is less reliable because it has a stake. Why: nothing in the passage questions the ministry's motives or ranks forecasters by their interests. Why the others ARE mentioned: the last paragraph warns against treating the average as the truth (shared blind spot); the added paragraph on GDP and value added warns against comparing one with the other; paragraph 2 warns against taking the first announcement as settled. Tip: in NOT-questions, check each option against a specific paragraph.

questions.question: The difference between GDP and gross value added, as explained in the passage, arises because
options: gross value added includes the informal sector, which gross domestic product leaves out because its output is not recorded
gross domestic product is revised several times after its release, whereas gross value added is calculated only once
gross value added is measured by nowcasting models, and gross domestic product is measured by the official statisticians
GDP adds product taxes and subtracts subsidies to producers' value added, so changes in these can alter the gap
questions.explanation: Answer: GDP adds product taxes and subtracts subsidies to value added, so changes in these affect the gap. Why: the added paragraph says 'GDP adds taxes on products and subtracts subsidies to the value that producers add. A quarter in which subsidies rise, or in which tax collections lag, can therefore widen the gap'. Why the others fail: nothing says GDP excludes the informal sector; revision of one but not the other is not stated; and both figures are forecast and later officially measured. Tip: definitions in passages are usually given in a single sentence beginning with the term or its cause.

questions.question: The primary purpose of the passage is to
options: argue that the Keynesian approach to economic stabilisation was mistaken from the beginning and has never served any government well
describe the lives and careers of the two economists who were awarded the prize for work on economic stabilisation this year
explain why models built on the reasons for behaviour can predict responses to new policies better than those built on past aggregates
show that central banks should avoid making statements about future interest rates because such statements confuse households
questions.explanation: Answer: to explain why models built on reasons for behaviour predict policy responses better than those built on past aggregates. Why: paragraphs 2 and 3 contrast aggregate relationships that 'shift beneath the policymaker's hand' with a model that 'knows why people act'; the last paragraph says such theory 'will usually travel better'. Why the others fail: paragraph 1 says the recipe 'worked well' for three decades, so 'mistaken from the beginning' is wrong; the passage gives no biography; and paragraph 4 treats statements about future rates as a useful tool. Tip: purpose = what the whole passage does, not what its opening anecdote is about.

questions.question: According to the passage, the old method failed in the 1970s because
options: it assumed that measured relationships between aggregates were stable levers, although they depended on expectations that change when policy changes
it assumed that households and firms would not change their spending when the government changed its taxes
it relied entirely on the models of individual households, which cannot describe how an economy behaves as a whole
it was applied only in the years after the Great Depression, when demand had fallen too far to be raised again
questions.explanation: Answer: it treated measured aggregate relationships as stable levers, though they depend on expectations that shift when policy shifts. Why: paragraph 2 says the old method 'assumed that these relationships were stable' and that 'When policy changes, expectations change, and the relationships ... may shift'. Why the others fail: the failing method is the AGGREGATE one, not the household-based one the laureates built; there is no claim that the old approach assumed spending would not change; and paragraph 1 says the formula was used for three decades after the Depression. Tip: the 'difficulty' sentence is usually the cause the question asks for.

questions.question: The example of a government that tolerates more inflation in order to reduce unemployment is used to show that
options: governments should never tolerate inflation, since it always fails to reduce unemployment even for a short time
workers and firms are unable to form expectations about prices unless the central bank announces its future rates
the relationship between inflation and unemployment has never existed in any country at any time in history
a pattern in past data may vanish once people anticipate a policy designed to exploit it
questions.explanation: Answer: a pattern seen in past data may vanish when people anticipate the policy meant to exploit it. Why: the paragraph says the pattern 'was real, but it depended on people not anticipating the policy that was designed to exploit it'. Why the others fail: 'never' and 'always' overstate; the passage says the relationship was real in past data; and the central bank's announcements are a separate point in paragraph 4. Tip: 'was real, but' signals the author's qualification.

questions.question: The passage suggests that a statement by a central bank about the likely path of interest rates can affect spending today because
options: the central bank has the legal power to compel households and firms to spend more than they would otherwise have chosen
households and firms form expectations about future rates, and these expectations influence decisions even if the current rate does not change
such a statement raises current interest rates directly by changing the price at which banks borrow from the central bank
households and firms ignore the current rate and therefore respond only to statements that concern the distant future
questions.explanation: Answer: expectations about future rates shape decisions today even without a change in the current rate. Why: paragraph 4 says 'If households and firms form expectations about future interest rates, then a statement about the likely path of those rates can influence spending today, without any change in the rate itself.' Why the others fail: there is no compulsion; the statement works 'without any change in the rate'; and 'ignore the current rate' overstates the claim. Tip: 'without any change in' tells you what the effect does NOT depend on.

questions.question: Which of the following can be inferred from the final paragraph?
options: A bottom-up model with unrealistic assumptions about how people reason may fail, however elegant its structure
Models built on past correlations are always less accurate than models built on the decisions of individuals
A model derived from household and firm decisions is free of the need to make any assumptions about behaviour
The laureates have conceded that their approach is no better than the older one that it replaced
questions.explanation: Answer: a bottom-up model with unrealistic assumptions may fail, however elegant. Why: the paragraph says assumptions that are 'unrealistic' mean 'the elegance of the structure will not save it', and that such theory travels well 'only if the reasons it assumes are close to the reasons that people really have'. Why the others fail: it says such models 'usually' travel better, not always; the paragraph states that they DO need assumptions; and nothing says the laureates concede equality with the older approach. Tip: the words 'usually' and 'only if' set limits that wrong options remove.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most WEAKEN the author's argument that models built on the reasons for behaviour travel better than those built on past correlations?
options: Economists who use aggregate relationships are generally older than those who use models built on individual decisions
Households and firms in several countries changed their expectations after central banks began to publish their forecasts
Across many policy changes, models built on aggregate relationships predicted outcomes more accurately than models built on household decisions, whose assumptions about reasoning proved poor
A few central banks have stopped using any formal model and now rely on the judgement of their own senior officials alone
questions.explanation: Answer: if aggregate models did better in practice because the bottom-up assumptions were poor, the author's claim is directly weakened. Why: the passage claims that reason-based models 'will usually travel better', but only if their assumptions are realistic; evidence that their assumptions failed in practice and aggregate models outperformed them attacks the claim itself. Why the others do not weaken: the age of economists is irrelevant; changing expectations after forecasts are published supports the expectations argument; and abandoning formal models says nothing about which kind is better. Tip: to weaken a comparison, show the opposite result in practice.

questions.question: Which of the following best states the main point of the passage?
options: India's electric vehicle market has failed to grow in any meaningful way, because the share of electric vehicles in sales has fallen
Growth statistics answer different questions, such as volume and share, so ask growth of what, against what base, relative to which alternative
Governments should measure the success of their policies by the number of electric vehicles sold, and not by the share of all sales
Rapid growth of a new technology in its early stage is certain to continue until the technology has replaced every older rival
questions.explanation: Answer: growth statistics answer different questions, so ask growth of what, against what base and relative to which alternative. Why: the opening says the two statements 'answer different questions'; the final sentence lists those three questions. Why the others fail: the passage says volume rose strongly, so 'failed to grow' is wrong; paragraph 3 says that for emissions policy, penetration matters more; and paragraph 5 warns that growth rates early in a technology's life are 'less impressive than they appear'. Tip: the closing question often summarises the passage.

questions.question: According to the passage, penetration can fall even while volume rises if
options: the total market grows faster than the electric segment does
the government stops offering any support to buyers of electric vehicles in the later part of the year
the number of charging points grows more slowly than the number of electric vehicles on the road
manufacturers sell electric vehicles at a lower price than they charge for petrol and diesel vehicles
questions.explanation: Answer: when the total market grows faster than the electric segment. Why: paragraph 2 says 'Volume can rise while penetration falls if the total market grows faster than the electric segment'. Why the others fail: policy support, charging points and relative prices are not given as the condition in this arithmetic; the passage later says relative prices matter, but for adoption, not for this ratio. Tip: when a question asks for the 'if' condition, find the sentence that states it.

questions.question: The author mentions the shop whose sales of a product double while the market triples in order to show that
options: a shop that doubles its sales of a product has necessarily made the most successful decision in the whole market
a product whose market triples must be an electric vehicle, since only such a market can grow so quickly
the shop owner should be less concerned with the market than with the sales that he made in the previous year
growth in absolute terms can coexist with a loss of share, since what matters is the growth of the whole market
questions.explanation: Answer: absolute growth can coexist with loss of share when the whole market grows faster. Why: paragraph 2 says the shop 'is losing ground relative to its rivals if the whole market has tripled'. Why the others fail: the shop has not necessarily done well; the example is generic ('any growing market'), not specific to electric vehicles; and the owner is not advised to ignore the market. Tip: an example generalises the previous sentence's arithmetic.

questions.question: Which of the following is a likely consequence of judging a policy by volume alone, according to the passage?
options: The policy will be abandoned too early, because volume figures always understate the progress of a new technology in its early stage of growth
The policy will be judged by the wrong body, since volume figures are collected by manufacturers and not by the government
The policy may look successful without changing the market's composition, which is what matters for fuel use and emissions
The policy will be applied to a market that has already reached saturation, where further growth in volume is impossible
questions.explanation: Answer: the policy may look successful without changing the market's composition. Why: paragraph 3 says 'A policy that is judged by volume may look successful even as it fails to alter the composition of the market', and that fuel use depends on the fleet's share. Why the others fail: volume figures are not said to understate; nothing is said about who collects them; and saturation is introduced later as a stage of the S-curve, not as a consequence of volume-based judgement. Tip: pick the consequence the paragraph itself states.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the 'base effect' discussed in the passage?
options: A decline in the share of a product in the market when the total market has grown faster than the product itself has done
The tendency of new technologies to grow slowly at first, then quickly, and finally to level off as they approach saturation in the market
The effect of a change in indirect taxes on the relative price of a technology and of the older products that compete with it
A modest increase on a small starting figure gives a large percentage growth, while the same increase on a larger base gives much less
questions.explanation: Answer: a modest absolute increase on a small base gives a large percentage, and much less on a larger base. Why: paragraph 4 defines it: 'when that figure is small, a modest increase in absolute terms produces a large percentage'.
