Why the others fail: they describe, in turn, penetration (paragraph 2), the S-shaped path (the added paragraph) and the effect of tax cuts on rivals (the last paragraph). Tip: three of the options are other ideas from the same passage; match the definition to the term.

questions.question: The reference to electric two-wheelers cooling after indirect tax cuts on petrol and diesel vehicles illustrates that
options: a technology's progress depends on the relative price of its rivals, as well as on its own merits
tax cuts on older products always prevent a new technology from achieving any growth in the market
electric cars and three-wheelers are less sensitive to price than two-wheelers because they are used for work
the share of electric vehicles in sales is unaffected by the price of petrol and diesel vehicles in the market
questions.explanation: Answer: a technology's progress depends on the relative price of rivals, not only its own merits. Why: the final paragraph says 'A technology's progress, in other words, depends on the relative price of what it competes with, as well as on its own merits.' Why the others fail: it says momentum 'cooled' for two-wheelers while cars and three-wheelers continued to grow, so 'always prevent' is wrong; the explanation about work use is not given; and the share is shown to be affected. Tip: 'in other words' introduces the author's own summary of the example.

questions.question: Dr. Anand's remark that the ninety per cent figure 'is a measure of imitation, not of quality' implies that
options: the tool is likely to be inaccurate, because it cannot match the decisions of recruiters in more than nine cases out of ten
the vendor has deliberately exaggerated the performance of the tool in order to persuade companies to buy it
agreement with past recruiters shows the tool copies them, and says nothing about whether they chose good employees
recruiters who have worked for many years always choose better employees than any statistical tool can choose
questions.explanation: Answer: agreement with past recruiters shows imitation, and says nothing about whether those recruiters chose well. Why: he says 'it has learnt to do what the recruiters did' and 'Whether those recruiters picked good employees is a separate question that the figure does not answer'. Why the others fail: ninety per cent agreement is not described as inaccurate; he does not accuse the vendor of exaggeration; and he does not claim recruiters always choose better. Tip: when a speaker separates two questions, the wrong options merge them.

questions.question: According to Dr. Anand, the pattern in which graduates of smaller colleges are ranked low is 'reinforced by its own output' because
options: the tool is programmed by the vendor to prefer graduates of larger colleges over all other candidates
such graduates are never interviewed, so the firm never learns how they would have performed, and the data keeps recording their absence
the graduates of smaller colleges perform badly after they are hired, and the tool has learnt from that record
recruiters are required by law to follow the tool's ranking and cannot interview candidates it has ranked low
questions.explanation: Answer: such graduates are never interviewed, so the firm never learns how they would have done and the data keeps recording their absence. Why: he says 'we shall never learn whether they would have done well, because they were never given the chance'. Why the others fail: he does not say the vendor programmed a preference; there is no record of poor performance, since they were not hired; and legal compulsion is not mentioned. Tip: self-reinforcing patterns come from missing evidence, not from bad intent.

questions.question: Dr. Anand's proposed remedy is to
options: test the tool against how those hired later performed, and let a few screened-out candidates through, at some cost
abandon such tools altogether, since their agreement with past decisions makes them unfit to be used by any firm
retrain the tool each year on the latest hiring decisions so that it agrees with recruiters more than ninety per cent of the time
ask the vendor to publish the method by which the tool was trained, so that any bias in it may be removed in advance
questions.explanation: Answer: test against outcomes and let some screened-out candidates through, accepting the cost. Why: he says 'The remedy is not to abandon such tools, but to test them against outcomes ... and to allow a small number of candidates through who would have been screened out', and calls the cost 'the price of knowing'. Why the others fail: he explicitly rejects abandoning; retraining on recruiters' choices would deepen imitation; publication of method is not proposed. Tip: 'not X, but Y' means Y is the speaker's view.

questions.question: His ________ inspection, a glance at the cover and a quick nod, was so careless that the forged signature on the last page went unnoticed.
options: meticulous
exhaustive
perfunctory
rigorous
questions.explanation: Answer: 'perfunctory' means done as a duty, with minimal care or effort. The clue is 'a glance at the cover and a quick nod' and the missed forgery. The others: 'meticulous' (extremely careful), 'exhaustive' (thorough, covering everything) and 'rigorous' (strict, thorough) are all opposite to careless. Tip: when the outcome is a missed detail, the blank is a word for carelessness.

questions.question: The company's ________ attitude towards safety, in which it spent only the legal minimum and grudged even that, led to its being criticised by the inspectors.
options: profligate
parsimonious
munificent
extravagant
questions.explanation: Answer: 'parsimonious' means unwilling to spend, extremely thrifty. The clue is 'spent only the legal minimum and grudged even that'. The others: 'profligate' (wastefully extravagant), 'munificent' (very generous) and 'extravagant' (spending excessively) all describe spending freely. Tip: 'grudged' signals unwillingness to give or spend.

questions.question: Being ________ about procedure, the clerk returned the entire application because a single date had been written in the wrong format.
options: cavalier
lax
indifferent
punctilious
questions.explanation: Answer: 'punctilious' means very careful about correct details and rules. The clue is that an entire application was returned over 'a single date ... in the wrong format'. The others: 'cavalier' (casual and dismissive), 'lax' (not strict) and 'indifferent' (not caring) would not lead someone to reject a form over such a detail. Tip: an extreme reaction to a tiny error signals extreme attention to detail.

questions.question: The forecast was ________ with caveats: it gave a range and not a single figure, and the authors ________ readers not to treat the midpoint as a ________.
options: hedged; urged; prediction
hedged; cautioned; prediction
unqualified; cautioned; prediction
hedged; cautioned; certainty
questions.explanation: Answer: hedged; cautioned; prediction. Step by step. A forecast 'with caveats' that gives a range is 'hedged' (qualified); the authors 'cautioned' (warned) readers not to treat the midpoint as a single 'prediction'. 'Urged' readers not to would not make sense with 'not to treat'; 'unqualified' contradicts 'with caveats'; 'certainty' would make the warning odd, since a midpoint of a range is never described as a certainty. Tip: 'range and not a single figure' tells you the report is qualified.

questions.question: A ________ market is one in which prices change sharply from day to day, so a trader who is ________ by one bad session may sell at the bottom and ________ a loss that patience would have avoided.
options: volatile; unnerved; crystallise
volatile; reassured; crystallise
stagnant; unnerved; crystallise
volatile; unnerved; recoup
questions.explanation: Answer: volatile; unnerved; crystallise. Step by step. Prices that change sharply make a 'volatile' market; a trader frightened ('unnerved') by one bad session sells at the bottom and thereby 'crystallises' (makes real) a loss. 'Reassured' would not lead to panic selling; 'stagnant' (not moving) contradicts sharp changes; 'recoup' (win back) contradicts 'a loss that patience would have avoided'. Tip: 'sell at the bottom' tells you the trader was frightened.

questions.question: The minister's speech was full of ________ promises: each sounded generous, yet none was ________ by a date or a budget, so the audience had little reason to ________ that anything would change.
options: amorphous; underwritten; doubt
concrete; underwritten; expect
amorphous; contradicted; expect
amorphous; underwritten; expect
questions.explanation: Answer: amorphous; underwritten; expect. Step by step. Promises with no date or budget are shapeless and vague ('amorphous'); none was 'underwritten' (backed, guaranteed) by a date or a budget; so the audience had little reason to 'expect' change. 'Doubt' would reverse the logic of 'little reason to ...'; 'concrete' contradicts 'no date or budget'; 'contradicted' is not what the clause 'by a date or a budget' describes. Tip: 'little reason to ___' needs the thing that would normally be believed.

questions.question: Although the study was widely cited as ________ proof that the programme worked, its sample was so small and so ________ that a careful reader would call its findings merely ________.
options: irrefutable; unrepresentative; definitive
tentative; unrepresentative; suggestive
irrefutable; unrepresentative; suggestive
irrefutable; comprehensive; suggestive
questions.explanation: Answer: irrefutable; unrepresentative; suggestive. Step by step. 'Although' signals contrast: cited as 'irrefutable' (impossible to disprove) proof, but with a small, 'unrepresentative' sample, so a careful reader would call the findings merely 'suggestive' (pointing towards but not proving). 'Definitive' would not be 'merely'; 'tentative' would not contrast with 'Although'; 'comprehensive' (covering everything) contradicts a small sample. Tip: 'merely' calls for a weaker word.

questions.question: Far from ________ criticism, the editor ________ it, and the paper's reputation for accuracy grew because mistakes were corrected ________ and not buried.
options: welcoming; solicited; promptly
resenting; ignored; promptly
resenting; solicited; promptly
resenting; solicited; grudgingly
questions.explanation: Answer: resenting; solicited; promptly. Step by step. 'Far from ___ criticism' needs a negative attitude the editor did NOT have: 'resenting'. The editor 'solicited' (asked for) it, and mistakes were corrected 'promptly' and not buried. 'Welcoming' would not contrast with 'far from'; 'ignored' contradicts the growing reputation; 'grudgingly' contradicts the favourable picture. Tip: 'far from X-ing, did Y' means Y is the opposite of X.

questions.question: The minister moved to ________ the tension, the report ________ to earlier failures without naming them, and the officials involved managed to ________ any blame.
options: diffuse; alluded; elude
defuse; eluded; allude
diffuse; eluded; allude
defuse; alluded; elude
questions.explanation: Answer: defuse; alluded; elude. DEFUSE means to make less dangerous (a tension, a bomb); DIFFUSE means to spread out. ALLUDE means to refer to indirectly; ELUDE means to escape or avoid. So the minister moves to 'defuse' tension, the report 'alluded' to failures without naming them, and the officials managed to 'elude' blame. Tip: you allude to a thing; you elude a pursuer.

questions.question: The auditor chose to ________ the earlier ruling, visited the ________ of the dispute, and was shocked by the ________ that met her.
options: cite; site; sight
site; cite; sight
cite; sight; site
sight; site; cite
questions.explanation: Answer: cite; site; sight. CITE means to quote or refer to as evidence (a ruling); SITE is a place or location; SIGHT is something seen, or the faculty of seeing. So the auditor cites the ruling, visits the site and is shocked by the sight. Tip: a 'site' is a location; a 'sight' is something you see.

questions.question: The new law will ________ the use of the chemical outright, though a doctor may still ________ a substitute, and the report did not ________ that the substitute was entirely harmless.
options: prescribe; proscribe; imply
proscribe; prescribe; imply
proscribe; prescribe; infer
prescribe; prescribe; infer
questions.explanation: Answer: proscribe; prescribe; imply. PROSCRIBE means to forbid; PRESCRIBE means to order or recommend (a medicine, a rule). A law forbids ('proscribe') the chemical; a doctor orders ('prescribe') a substitute. IMPLY means to suggest without stating; INFER means to conclude from evidence. The report did not 'imply' (suggest) harmlessness. The other options swap the first pair or use 'infer' for a writer's act. Tip: the writer implies; the reader infers.

questions.question: One of the statements below contains a word used incorrectly or inappropriately. Choose the option which has the incorrect or inappropriate usage of the word.
options: Her long pause in reply seemed to imply that she disagreed.
The audience inferred from her long pause that she disagreed.
Do you mean to imply that the figures were altered?
From the long pause in her reply, the audience implied that she disagreed.
questions.explanation: Answer: the sentence 'the audience implied'. IMPLY is what a speaker or writer does (suggests without stating); INFER is what a listener or reader does (concludes from evidence). The audience, receiving the pause, 'inferred'. The other sentences are correct: 'her pause ... imply', 'the audience inferred' and 'mean to imply'. Tip: the sender implies; the receiver infers.

questions.question: The prize was shared between <u>he and her</u>, who had worked together for twenty years.
options: he and she
him and she
him and her
his and her
questions.explanation: Answer: 'him and her'. Rule: after a preposition ('between'), pronouns take the object case: him and her. 'Between he and her' mixes cases; 'he and she' and 'him and she' use the subject form 'she' after a preposition; 'his and her' is possessive and has no noun to follow. Tip: after a preposition, use object pronouns (me, him, her, us, them).

questions.question: Hardly had the results been announced <u>than</u> the markets began to react.
options: when
then
that
as soon
questions.explanation: Answer: 'when'. Rule: 'Hardly' (and 'scarcely') takes 'when' (or 'before'); 'no sooner' takes 'than'. So 'Hardly had the results been announced when the markets began to react', or 'No sooner had the results been announced than ...'. 'Then' and 'that' are not correlatives of 'hardly'; 'as soon' is incomplete. Tip: hardly/scarcely ... when; no sooner ... than.

questions.question: She is one of the few economists who <u>has</u> predicted the slowdown correctly.
options: is
have
was being
having
questions.explanation: Answer: 'have'. Rule: in 'one of the few economists who ...', the relative pronoun 'who' refers to the plural 'economists' (not to 'one'), so the verb is plural: 'who have predicted'. 'Is' and 'was being' do not fit the sense or the tense; 'having' is a participle and cannot be the main verb of the clause. Tip: 'one of the + plural noun + who/which + plural verb'.

questions.question: This model is more accurate than <u>any other models</u> that the bank has used so far.
options: all other model
any others models
any other model
any of other model
questions.explanation: Answer: 'any other model'. Rule: a comparison of a thing with the rest of its class uses 'any other' followed by a SINGULAR noun ('any other model'), because 'any' picks out one at a time. 'Any other models' is a common error; 'all other model' mixes quantity and number; 'any others models' and 'any of other model' are ungrammatical. Tip: 'more ... than any other + singular noun'.

questions.question:
Complete the paragraph logically:

Two forecasting teams that use the same data can reach different estimates of growth. ____________________. For this reason, the spread among forecasts is better read as a measure of uncertainty than as a sign of error.
options: Each team must choose its indicators, weights and assumptions, and reasonable choices can lead to different answers.
One of the teams must be careless, since competent teams that use the same data would always reach the same estimate.
The official statisticians will publish the same figure as the forecasters, since all of them use the same sources.
The differences disappear when the teams meet, because the true figure is already known to each of them in advance.
questions.explanation: Answer: each team makes choices, and reasonable choices can differ. Why: the closing sentence says the spread is 'uncertainty' not 'error', which follows only if the differences come from legitimate choices. Why the others fail: blaming carelessness is the opposite of 'not a sign of error'; the claim that official figures will match is unsupported; and a known true figure would make forecasts unnecessary. Tip: 'For this reason' draws a conclusion from the blank.

questions.question:
Complete the paragraph logically:

Sales of a product can double while its share of the market falls. ____________________. A reader who looks only at the sales will therefore miss that the product is losing ground.
options: This happens only when the product is sold at a price that is lower than the price of every other product in the market.
This happens when the whole market grows faster than the product, so that the product's fraction of the total becomes smaller.
This cannot happen in practice, because a product whose sales have doubled must have gained share relative to the rest.
This happens because a falling share of the market always raises the sales of the product in the following year.
questions.explanation: Answer: it happens when the whole market grows faster than the product. Why: the next sentence says looking only at sales misses 'losing ground', which fits a case of faster overall growth. Why the others fail: price is irrelevant to the arithmetic; 'cannot happen' contradicts the opening sentence; and 'always raises sales' makes an unsupported causal claim. Tip: the blank must explain how the opening claim can be true.

questions.question:
Complete the paragraph logically:

A screening tool that has been trained on past hiring decisions will learn the patterns in those decisions, including any unfairness in them. ____________________. The firm therefore needs to test the tool against how the people it hired later performed.
options: Its agreement with past decisions proves that it is fair, since a tool that matches human choices cannot repeat their errors.
Its agreement with past decisions is of no importance, since a tool of this kind never uses data about earlier recruitment.
Its agreement with past decisions shows that recruiters will soon be unnecessary, since the tool can perform their work.
Its agreement with past decisions shows that it copies them, not that those decisions were sound.
questions.explanation: Answer: its agreement shows only that it copies past decisions, not that they were sound. Why: the next sentence says the firm must test the tool against later performance, because agreement with past choices cannot establish quality. Why the others fail: matching human choices means repeating their errors, so 'proves it is fair' is wrong; the tool DOES use past data; and replacing recruiters is a different point. Tip: 'therefore' in the following sentence signals that the blank states the problem to be tested.

questions.question:
Rearrange the five sentences (1-5) into a logical sequence (Type the 5-digit sequence as answer):

1. The first release is therefore a provisional judgement.
2. Some of the returns arrive late and incomplete, and the gaps are filled by estimates.
3. Official growth figures are not read from a counter; they are assembled.
4. Those estimates are revised when the missing data come in.
5. A forecaster should treat the first number as a starting point and not as the final answer.
questions.explanation: Answer: 3-2-4-1-5. Step by step. Sentence 3 opens with the general claim (assembled). Sentence 2 says why (late, incomplete returns, estimates). Sentence 4 begins 'Those estimates' and continues from the estimates in 2. Sentence 1 begins 'therefore' and concludes (provisional). Sentence 5 gives the advice that follows. Tip: 'Those estimates' needs 'estimates' mentioned just before.

questions.question:
Rearrange the five sentences (1-5) into a logical sequence (Type the 5-digit sequence as answer):

1. Volume and penetration therefore answer different questions.
2. Electric vehicle sales rose sharply in October.
3. Yet the share of electric vehicles in all sales fell in the same month.
4. That happened because the whole market grew faster than the electric segment.
5. A manufacturer planning a factory needs volume, while a policy-maker concerned with emissions needs share.
questions.explanation: Answer: 2-3-4-1-5. Step by step. Sentence 2 states the first fact (sales rose). Sentence 3 begins 'Yet' and gives the contrasting fact (share fell). Sentence 4 begins 'That happened because' and explains the contrast. Sentence 1 begins 'therefore' and draws the conclusion (different questions). Sentence 5 applies the conclusion to two users. Tip: 'Yet' follows a fact and introduces a contrast; 'therefore' follows the explanation.

questions.question:
Rearrange the four sentences (1-4) into a logical sequence (Type the 4-digit sequence as answer):

1. The relationships it measured, however, depended on what people expected.
2. The old method treated relationships between aggregates as stable levers.
3. When policy changed, expectations changed, and the relationships shifted.
4. A model built on the reasons for behaviour can anticipate such shifts.
questions.explanation: Answer: 2-1-3-4. Step by step. Sentence 2 introduces the old method and its assumption. Sentence 1 begins 'however' and says the relationships depended on expectations ('it' = the method). Sentence 3 describes what happened when policy changed. Sentence 4 offers the improved alternative ('such shifts' refers to the shifts in 3). Tip: 'such shifts' needs the shifts to have been described just before.

questions.question:
Rearrange the five sentences (1-5) into a logical sequence (Type the 5-digit sequence as answer):

1. The firm never learns whether they would have performed well.
2. A screening tool may rank graduates of smaller colleges low because they were rarely hired.
3. Those graduates are therefore rarely interviewed.
4. The tool's ranking then confirms itself, since the missing evidence is never collected.
5. The remedy is to let a few candidates through and watch how they perform.
questions.explanation: Answer: 2-3-1-4-5. Step by step. Sentence 2 introduces the ranking and its cause. Sentence 3 begins 'therefore' and gives the consequence (rarely interviewed). Sentence 1 follows: because they are not interviewed, the firm never learns how they would perform ('they' = those graduates). Sentence 4 says the pattern confirms itself, since evidence is missing. Sentence 5 offers the remedy. Tip: the remedy usually comes last.

questions.question:
Rearrange the four sentences (1-4) into a logical sequence (Type the 4-digit sequence as answer):

1. A single indicator, such as electricity use, may move for reasons unrelated to output.
2. Nowcasting therefore combines many indicators that are available quickly.
3. Official data on output arrive weeks or months after a quarter ends.
4. A model of this kind can find the pattern that the indicators share.
questions.explanation: Answer: 3-1-2-4. Step by step. Sentence 3 opens with the problem (official data arrive late). Sentence 1 introduces the quick substitute and its weakness (a single indicator is unreliable). Sentence 2 begins 'therefore' and presents the solution (combine many indicators). Sentence 4 begins 'A model of this kind' and says what the combined model can do. Tip: 'of this kind' follows the mention of the model type, here 'Nowcasting ... combines'.
